1	# Prune
     2	
     3	Goal: fewer tokens in the target, with every accepted cut shown to drop the score by less than a margin fixed before the first cut. Run the rest of the loop as in `SKILL.md`. Count tokens with `bun run skill-lint`.
     4	
     5	## Margin
     6	
     7	Before the first cut, write the margin in the climb log: the largest drop in with-arm pass rate a cut may cost. Read the noise columns from `Ready the Suite` and set the run count so a drop of the margin's size stars at `--alpha 0.2`, per the table in [screen.md](screen.md), since at lower power a harmful cut also fails to star.
     8	
     9	## Cuts
    10	
    11	Cut a rule: the sentences under one heading that produce one behavior. Its targets are the graders it was written for, and every other case is a guard. Cut only a rule a grader checks. For an unchecked rule, add a case that checks it and re-run the baseline, or leave it to the `prompting:prompting` relevance pass.
    12	
    13	Order cuts by tokens saved: the description first, since it costs every turn, then the body, then references.
    14	
    15	Batch cuts whose rules have disjoint targets into one candidate. When a batch fails, bisect it on the same base until one rule remains.
    16	
    17	## Blocks
    18	
    19	When the target contains a block of many rules, cut the whole block as the first candidate and verify it on the full suite. When it holds, accept it as one cut. When it fails, list the cases whose with-arm score dropped. Screen each rule's cut on those cases only, per [screen.md](screen.md), restore every rule whose screen drops, and verify the combined remaining cut on the full suite. That verify catches a rule that matters only beside another.
    20	
    21	## Hold
    22	
    23	Accept a cut when all of these hold on the pooled columns:
    24	
    25	- No with-arm cell stars down at `--alpha 0.2`.
    26	- Each target grader's with-arm pass rate falls by less than the margin.
    27	- The `dev` tag row's with-arm score falls by less than the margin.
    28	
    29	When a target falls to the without arm's rate, restore the rule and try a shorter wording as its own candidate.
    30	
    31	## Drift
    32	
    33	After every third accepted cut, and before the closing PR, compare the current commit against the original base's columns with the same margin. When the total drop exceeds it, bisect the accepted cuts and restore the costliest.
    34	
    35	At the end, run `holdout` on the original base and the final commit. The prune holds when `holdout` falls by less than the margin. The closing PR states the tokens before and after, the margin, and the `holdout` score on both commits.

1	# Screen
     2	
     3	A screen runs a candidate on its target and guard cases only, with many repeats in one invocation, to decide whether the candidate earns a full-suite verify. Power on a case comes from that case's run count. A full replicate spends most of its cost on cases the candidate never touches. A screen reaches the same per-case power in a fraction of the time.
     4	
     5	## Repeats
     6	
     7	At a base that passed all its runs on a case, the cell stars at p<0.1 only once the candidate fails about 5 runs, at any run count. Run about 5 ÷ the drop rate repeats a side:
     8	
     9	| Drop on one case | Repeats a side | Example |
    10	| --- | --- | --- |
    11	| all runs | 4 | 4/4 → 0/4, p=0.03 |
    12	| half | 8 to 10 | 8/8 → 4/8, p=0.08 |
    13	| a quarter | 16 to 20 | 16/16 → 12/16, p=0.10. 20/20 → 15/20, p=0.05 |
    14	
    15	A base one run below ceiling needs about two more failures to star. Raising alpha to 0.2 saves at most one failure at a ceiling base. Size a prune screen the same way. Size every screen from the smallest drop that would reject the candidate, since a smaller screen passes that regression.
    16	
    17	## Invocations
    18	
    19	Repeats inside one invocation share its drift: fixture setup, cache warmth, and the backend's state at that moment. A screen accepts that drift because its base side runs at the same moment and shares it. Run the two sides concurrently, or back to back, on the same harness version and model.
    20	
    21	A screen's repeats are less independent than replicates. Its p-values overstate confidence. A screen therefore decides only whether a candidate goes to verify, and never accepts. The verify columns pool separate invocations, where drift varies inside each column rather than between them.
    22	
    23	When cases mutate fixture state seeded once per invocation, repeats are not independent at all. Reset the fixture per repeat or screen with separate invocations.
    24	
    25	## Parallelism
    26	
    27	Use the harness's parallel workers inside each invocation. The slowest case and fixture setup bound wall time, and total agent time ÷ workers is the floor. Screens of several candidates can run at once, each beside its own base side or sharing one base side launched at the same moment.
    28	
    29	For verify, run the base and candidate sides of each replicate concurrently, and run the replicates one after another. Each pair then sees the same backend moment. Time drift lands on both columns instead of between them, and the pooled column still spans drift across pairs. Launching every replicate of both sides at once collapses them into one time slice, which is no better than in-invocation repeats.
    30	
    31	Concurrency adds its own failure modes:
    32	
    33	- Rate limits and timeouts error runs unevenly between sides. An errored run is void, per `Compare`.
    34	- Fixtures sharing a port, a database, or a working directory collide across invocations. Give each invocation its own.
    35	- Latency and cost rise under load. Compare them only between runs at the same concurrency.
    36	- The native runner names a result directory by the second plus `--ref` or `--label`. Give concurrent runs distinct labels.
    37	
    38	## When to Skip
    39	
    40	Skip the screen when the target and guard cases make up most of the suite, since the screen then costs as much as the verify. Skip it for a reach candidate whose guards are the quiet cases across the suite.

1	# Ready the Suite
     2	
     3	A suite is ready when every check below holds. A climb on an unready suite measures the harness.
     4	
     5	- **Frame.** Name the artifact under test, the behavior it should produce, and the failure that motivated the suite: a user correction, a review comment, or a production failure, quoted from where it happened. Write the frame at the top of the suite's `README.md`, so every case and grader traces back to it. A suite with no motivating failure has no target to climb, so ask for one before writing a case.
     6	- **Source.** Take cases in this order: real turns the user corrected, then turns where the artifact fired or should have, then requests production traces show it handled badly, then bug repros that fail before the fix and pass after, then review comments. Synthesize a case only as a variation of a real one. Where the harness has its own miner, use it on session transcripts. Rewrite each mined turn into a fixture that keeps its shape and drops private content.
     7	- **Split.** Tag every case `dev` or `holdout` in its `case.yaml`. Candidates run on `dev`. `holdout` runs once, at the end, so no edit is tuned against it, and a climb that reads it again needs fresh `holdout` cases first. Assign the split at random within each kind of request, about a third to `holdout`, and never by baseline score, since cases picked for failing regress toward the mean. Give both splits a case for every kind of request the skill handles, so a `dev` guard catches a rule that bleeds from one kind into another. A suite too small to spare a `holdout` case per kind skips the split and reports its result as `dev`-only.
     8	- **Reach.** A case moves only when the skill fires on it. Add a `tool_used` grader on `Skill` with `input_match` naming the skill: under ablation it reports as an unscored indicator. Include cases where the skill should stay quiet, so a trigger change has a guard. The `Skill` indicator never scores, so guard a quiet case with a `trace` regex, `not_contains` on `"skill":"<name>"`. For a skill users invoke by name, simulate the invocation in `append_system_prompt` on every case, since there is no trigger to test.
     9	- **Balance.** Include cases where the skill should change little, so a climb that over-applies the skill loses score.
    10	- **Graders.** Grade the output with `regex` wherever a pattern decides it, and keep `llm` graders to one criterion each, with an example of a passing reply phrased differently from the obvious one, since the judge reads a bare criterion narrowly. Pair each removal grader with a survival grader for the fact that must stay, so deleting everything fails. Where a case invites invention, grade the claim of the likeliest plausible mechanism the fixture lacks, since a reply may rightly name it as ruled out. Test a claim pattern against negated forms ("haven't reproduced it"). Grade the end state or the reply, and keep `trace` graders for process guardrails such as a tool that must not run. Grade only what the prompt states or a domain expert would read into it, so two experts reach the same verdict on a reply.
    11	- **Judges.** Hand-grade the smoke run's replies against each `llm` grader before the baseline. Rewrite a grader that disagrees with your grade on more than one reply in ten. Set `judge_model` in `suite.yaml` to a model other than the one the climb runs, so the judge does not share its blind spots.
    12	- **Trace.** Match a tool call's input by its key and value alone. Key order in the serialized input varies by tool (`Edit` writes `replace_all` before `file_path`), so an anchored pattern can silently match nothing. Match a string value with `(?:[^"\\]|\\.)*`, since commands carry escaped quotes.
    13	- **Scope.** When the reply wraps an artifact in commentary, have `append_system_prompt` ask for the artifact inside `<out>` tags and anchor each regex to that block, or a report that quotes a cut phrase fails its own grader. Scope a positional `llm` grader ("the first sentence") the same way, or tell the judge which part of the reply to read. `<out>(?:(?!</out>)[\s\S])*?PATTERN` finds a pattern inside the block, and `<out>(?:(?!</out>)[\s\S]){N}` holds when the block runs past N characters, a floor under `contains` and a ceiling under `not_contains`. Size N per case, since a case with more moving parts earns a longer on-topic caveat.
    14	- **Isolation.** Stub every external service in the fixture: a bare repo for pushes, pasted text for API bodies, an `append_system_prompt` fallback telling the session what to reply when a network call fails. A run that dies on the network scores the sandbox. Keep graders, expected values, and other cases out of the fixture a session runs in, including its git history, since a `Read`, `Grep`, or `git log` finds them. A case whose right answer is "no cause found" needs a fixture with no latent cause: have a strong model hunt it before the baseline. A headless session lacks interactive tools such as `EnterPlanMode` and `AskUserQuestion` even when granted. Grade a step that uses one by its observable effect, and tell the session through `append_system_prompt` that nobody answers mid-task.
    15	- **Wrap.** An artifact outside a plugin (a user skill, an agent, a rule or `CLAUDE.md`) loads through the `wrap` key in the suite's `suite.yaml`, which the runner builds into a throwaway plugin. Context files reach the session through a `SessionStart` hook, whatever their `paths:` frontmatter says.
    16	- **Lint.** Run `shellcheck` on the scaffold scripts, and test each regex grader with `bun evals/native/check.ts <suite>` against examples: one that should pass every grader, one per grader that should fail it, and an empty reply that fails every survival grader. Trace graders need `.jsonl` examples: hand-write them on the model of a smoke run's `tool_use` lines, serialized as compact JSON (`"key":"value"`, as `JSON.stringify` writes it), since trace patterns match that form. Hand-write replies for the `holdout` cases. A fix after the baseline edits a case mid-climb.
    17	- **Scaling.** Run the unchanged `dev` cases once with `--model` set a tier above the climb's model. A case that scores lower there, or fails every run on both arms there, grades an artifact of the fixture or the grader rather than the task: fix it before the baseline.
    18	- **Noise.** Run the unchanged `dev` cases twice with an explicit `--runs` (the runner defaults to 3), priced first per `Running` at 2 × runs × the per-run cost. Compare the two with `compare.ts`. Stars there are noise at that run count, and they set how many runs a candidate needs. `compare.ts` marks a cell below 4 runs a side `†`, so zero stars at fewer runs says nothing about noise. A case whose without arm swings across its range between noise columns needs more pooled runs than the rest. A grader that fails on both arms in every run is a harness artifact until a trace shows otherwise, such as a `file_exists` glob matching the sandbox's own dotfiles. Scope file globs to what a session would write. A stray `Agent` call can leave a trailing message after the reply, and a `last_message` grader grades that message, so open the trace behind a lone with-arm drop before counting it. `allowed_tools` does not remove `Agent`.
    19	- **Headroom.** A case at 1.00 on both arms in the noise runs discriminates nothing. Harden or replace it until the with arm has room to rise and the without arm sits below it. Aim the new graders at what a user corrected or a reviewer judged wrong in real use, since graders aimed at whatever the without arm fails today measure one model's blind spots rather than the task. Balance cases are exempt. A suite ported from rubric asserts saturates this way. When a hardening round leaves the with arm at 1.00 again, stop hardening: the skill already handles those cases, and the suite ships as a regression guard.

     2	name: friction

    13	# Friction
    14	
    15	Find what keeps slowing the setup down. Every symptom here recurs. Mid-week, only a blocker with a small fix is worth a change. Everything else waits for the weekly list, ranked by how many days it persisted.
    16	
    17	The output budget is the point of this skill. A run that surfaces nothing is a correct run. Never pad.
    18	
    19	## Arguments
    20

    43	| Source | Window | How |
    44	| --- | --- | --- |
    45	| osquery | both | `collect.sh osquery`. How to read each query and name its target: [references/osquery.md](references/osquery.md) |
    46	| Atuin | both | `collect.sh atuin`: slow and failing command heads. [references/atuin.md](references/atuin.md) |
    47	| Session index | both | `observability:session` named queries with `after_date` at the window start. Daily: `tool-failure-rates`, `hook-blocks`, `hook-block-then-retry-success`, `sandbox-bypass-scaffold`, `cli-health`, `stop-hook-noop-detector`. Weekly runs every named query. It sees only local transcripts, so a quiet index means work moved to cloud sessions, not that friction stopped |
    48	| Changelogs | `7d` | Release notes since the last run for tools the config repos install that the window's data shows in use |
    49	
    50	Normalize every metric to a rate: per active hour, per call, or a share of minutes. Activity swings 200x day to day, so a raw count compares nothing.
    51	
    52	### 2. Ground
    53	
    54	Check each candidate against the live config in the config repos (`${user_config.config_repos}`), or the config files the tool reads when none are set. Drop any the config already addresses. A fix that does less work (skip a job, lower a limit) is not a fix here. Look for the change that makes the same work faster or attributes it.
    55	
    56	### 3. Emit Findings
    57	
    58	First read the open targets, so a symptom seen before keeps its fingerprint:
    59	
    60	```bash
    61	bun "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/ledger.ts" status
    62	```
    63	
    64	Reuse an entry's exact `type` and `target` when it describes the same symptom, even when you would word it differently. Otherwise take the target from the query's row in [osquery.md](references/osquery.md#targets) or [atuin.md](references/atuin.md#targets). For a session-index finding, the target is the hook script, tool, or command head the query names.
    65	
    66	One JSON object per symptom seen in the window, including ones you expect to stay quiet:
    67	
    68	```json
    69	{"type": "contention", "target": "bun, duckdb", "impact": "high",
    70	 "metric": "60% of saturated minutes had a bun/duckdb job within 2 min, vs 4% of other minutes",
    71	 "fix": "rebuild session-index views per touched session", "small": false}
    72	```
    73	
    74	- `type`: `contention`, `slow-command`, `failing-command`, `tool-gap`, `upstream-change`, `config-drift`.
    75	- `target`: the object the symptom is about, named the same way every run: a process name, a command head (its first two words, `g pull`, never its arguments), a tool, a hook script. The fingerprint is `type|target`, so a renamed target restarts its count.
    76	- `impact`: decides what surfaces, so grade it by what the symptom costs the user, not by how often it fires.
    77	  - `high`: blocks work. A command keeps failing through retries until someone works around it, or work stalls for minutes. Example: an auth command failing 9 of 11 runs across 25 minutes of retries.
    78	  - `moderate`: costs time or attention, but work recovers on its own. Examples: a hook rejection that costs Claude one retry turn, a minute added to each turn, commit signing failures that a retry clears.
    79	  - `low`: measurable but unnoticed. Low never surfaces. Record it so growth shows.
    80	
    81	  Skip a guard firing as designed (a write-block hook stopping a write it should stop). It is not friction.
    82	- `metric`: the one number behind the finding, with its query named.
    83	- `small`: true only when the fix is one PR of a handful of lines in one topic, with no new dependency, and reverts cleanly.
    84	
    85	Never put command arguments, paths under a work directory, or file contents in a finding. The ledger may leave the machine.
    86	
    87	### 4. Record
    88	
    89	Pipe the array to the ledger. It appends the day's findings, counts distinct days per fingerprint, and prints the decision:
    90	
    91	```bash
    92	echo "$FINDINGS" | bun "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/ledger.ts" record --window 1d
    93	```
    94	
    95	Do not count, rank, or override the decision yourself. The rules it applies:
    96	
    97	- Daily: promotes at most one entry seen today with `impact: high` and `small: true`. Moderate never promotes mid-week, however often it recurs.
    98	- Weekly: ranks every open entry by days seen, then impact, and promotes the top 5.
    99	- Filed and picked fingerprints wait for their outcome. Dismissed ones stay quiet for 30 days. A resolved one that returns is flagged `regression`.
   100	
   101	### 5. Deliver
   102	
   103	Daily, when `promote` holds an entry: implement the fix in the config repo that owns it and open a draft PR through `pull-request:create`, with `Friction: <fp>` on its own line in the body and the metric as evidence. Then record it:
   104	
   105	```bash
   106	bun "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/ledger.ts" outcome <fp> filed --ref <pr-url>
   107	```
   108	
   109	Weekly: write one ranked list, highest first. Each entry gives the target, days seen, the metric, the proposed change, and whether it is small.
   110	
   111	Both windows end the run's output with **Below the cut**: each `belowCut` entry as one line with its fingerprint, days seen, metric, and proposed change. The user picks from it with `pick <fingerprint>`. When the decision is empty, the whole output is one line saying the run found nothing to surface, plus how close the contention checks came: `saturation`'s `min_idle_pct` and the top `write-rate` name with its `peak_gb_per_min`.
   112	
   113	## Outcomes
   114	
   115	When a `Friction:` PR merges, record `resolved`. When the user closes one unmerged, record `dismissed`.

1	# Git Plugin
     2	
     3	Git workflow and branching best practices for Claude Code.
     4	
     5	## Contents
     6	
     7	- **Skills**:
     8	  - `conflicts`: Resolve git merge conflicts during rebase, merge, or cherry-pick. Drives the operation to completion and pushes when asked.
     9	- **Hooks**:
    10	  - Blocks direct commits to the default branch
    11	  - Records `git push -u` tracking outside the sandbox, which denies the `.git/config` write a linked worktree's push makes
    12	  - Refuses an `EnterWorktree` call the harness would reject
    13	  - Recovers a failed git network operation over HTTPS when the SSH agent refuses to sign
    14	  - Handles a refused commit or tag signature: asks for approval where signing is required, retries unsigned elsewhere
    15	
    16	## HTTPS Fallback
    17	
    18	[Secretive](https://github.com/maxgoedjen/secretive) gates every SSH signature behind Touch ID, so an unattended `git fetch`, `pull`, or `push` gets `agent refused operation` and then `Permission denied (publickey)`, exiting 128. Ordinary fetches and pulls fail the same way.
    19	
    20	The `PostToolUseFailure` hook watches failing `git` commands for that signature. When the repository (or the command) names an SSH remote on a host whose CLI holds HTTPS credentials (the `https_hosts` option, default `github.com=gh,gitlab.com=glab`), it returns the same command rewritten to go over HTTPS:
    21	
    22	```
    23	git -c credential.helper= -c 'credential.helper=!gh auth git-credential' -c 'url.https://github.com/.insteadOf=git@github.com:' -c 'url.https://github.com/.insteadOf=ssh://git@github.com/' fetch origin
    24	```
    25	
    26	The hook suggests, it does not retry. Rewriting the URL through `insteadOf` rather than substituting the remote with a bare URL keeps the remote name, its refspecs, and its remote-tracking ref updates identical to the SSH attempt. The provider CLI's `auth git-credential` helper supplies the token for the duration of that one command, so nothing is written to the repository's config and no credential is stored or echoed. The leading `credential.helper=` resets the helper list so a stale keychain entry cannot win.
    27	
    28	A host outside `https_hosts` doesn't get a suggestion, since no known CLI could authenticate the retry. Add a self-hosted forge or enterprise domain as another `host=cli` pair whose CLI provides `auth git-credential`.
    29	
    30	Commit and tag signing go through `ssh-keygen -Y sign` instead, and HTTPS cannot replace a signature. The fallback stays silent on them, and the signing refusal hook handles them.
    31	
    32	## Signing Refusal
    33	
    34	With `gpg.format=ssh`, an SSH agent that is locked or wants approval for each signature refuses an unattended `git commit`, `tag`, or `rebase`, and `ssh-keygen` reports `Couldn't sign message (signer): agent refused operation`. The `PostToolUseFailure` hook recognizes that output and checks whether the repository requires signatures:
    35	
    36	- `git config claude.requireSigning true` in the repository
    37	- a `required_signatures` rule on the current branch, from GitHub's `rules/branches` API
    38	- for a tag, a ruleset targeting tags that requires signatures
    39	
    40	When signing is required, the hook tells the model to stop and ask the user to unlock or approve the agent. Otherwise it tells the model to retry with `-c commit.gpgsign=false`. A lookup that can't reach GitHub counts as not required, and the push then reports the rejection.
    41	
    42	## Enter Worktree
    43	
    44	The `PreToolUse` hook on `EnterWorktree` denies a `path` call the harness is certain to reject. Claude Code enters only a worktree of the session's own repository, refuses the current directory, and after the session's first switch it enters only paths under the main checkout's `.claude/worktrees/`. Worktrees made outside the harness, by `git worktree add` or a worktree manager, usually live elsewhere. A skill that enters one hits these rejections on every cross-repo or worktree-to-worktree switch before it falls back to `cd`. Repository identity comes from `git rev-parse --git-common-dir`. Whether the session has switched comes from the newest `worktree-state` record in the transcript, the harness's own record of it. A session that merely started in a linked worktree can still switch once, and the hook allows that. Anything it cannot resolve, including subagent calls, passes through to the harness.
    45	
    46	**Delete it** once the `tool-failure-rates` session query shows the "is not a registered worktree", "is not under", "does not exist, so", and "is the current working directory" `EnterWorktree` signatures gone, and the skills that call the tool make the same check first.
    47	
    48	The hook self-times into `~/.claude/hook-metrics/` through `scripts/hook-metrics.ts`, a checked copy of `user/scripts/hook-metrics.ts` that `scripts/copies.test.ts` keeps identical.
    49	
    50	## Testing
    51	
    52	```bash
    53	bun test plugins/git
    54	```

     3	description: Resolve git merge conflicts from a rebase, merge, or cherry-pick. Use also for a request to finish the operation and push, such as "fix conflicts and push".
     4	argument-hint: "[--push]"

     7	  - Read

    28	    - matcher: "Bash(git commit:*)|Bash(git rebase --continue:*)|Bash(git merge --continue:*)|Bash(git cherry-pick --continue:*)"
    29	      hooks:
    30	        - type: command
    31	          command: "bun ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/skills/conflicts/scripts/check-markers.ts"
    32	---
    33	
    34	# Git Conflicts
    35	
    36	Every conflicted file ends as the result both sides intended: each side's change preserved, the file coherent, and nothing dropped that the merged result does not account for. Resolve a conflict these rules do not cover to that standard. When the three versions do not reveal what each side intended, keep both sides and ask the user.
    37	
    38	## Status
    39	
    40	!`bun ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/skills/conflicts/scripts/status.ts`
    41	
    42	## Context
    43	
    44	!`bun ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/skills/conflicts/scripts/context.ts`
    45	
    46	## Upstream
    47	
    48	!`bun ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/skills/conflicts/scripts/upstream.ts`
    49	
    50	## Resolving
    51	
    52	For each conflicted file, read base, ours, and theirs (`git show :1:path`, `:2:path`, `:3:path`), edit the file to the merged result, then `git add` it.
    53	
    54	- Regenerate a generated file, such as a lockfile or a build artifact, from its source. Follow the project's `CLAUDE.md` for lockfile guidance.
    55	- When repeated rebases hit the same conflict, [references/rerere.md](references/rerere.md) records a resolution and replays it.
    56	
    57	Resolving is done when every conflicted file is staged and `git diff --cached --check` reports no conflict markers. Leave the commit, the continue, and the push to the user.
    58	
    59	## Completing the Operation
    60	
    61	Take the operation past the staged resolution only when the user asks for it: the `--push` argument, its alias `push`, or a request such as "fix conflicts and push". Then:
    62	
    63	1. When no rebase, merge, or cherry-pick is in progress and upstream has diverged, run `git merge origin/<default-branch>` to produce the conflicts. A clean merge goes straight to the push.
    64	2. Summarize the conflicts and confirm with `AskUserQuestion` before resolving 3 or more files, non-trivial code, or conflicts whose intent is ambiguous. Resolve without asking when the conflicts are generated files only, or fewer than 3 conflicts across 1-2 files with an obvious resolution.
    65	3. Before continuing, set aside the dirty files unrelated to the resolution, which `git status --porcelain` lists. The continue then commits only the resolution. Run `git stash push -m "conflicts: <branch>" -- <files>` for all of them at once, then record that entry's SHA from `git stash list --format='%H %gs'`. When that stash fails, which the sandbox causes by blocking the unlink of a protected file such as `.mcp.json`, stash the files one at a time and skip the failures. Hide each file that cannot be stashed with `git update-index --assume-unchanged <file>`.
    66	4. Continue the operation and run `git push`, then restore the files you set aside: `git update-index --no-assume-unchanged <file>` for each hidden file, and `git stash apply <sha>` then `git stash drop <sha>` for a stash you created. Restore by the SHA you recorded, because the stash stack is shared with every other worktree on the repo and the top entry may belong to another session.
    67	
    68	The operation is done when git reports no operation in progress, the branch is pushed, and every file you set aside is back in the working tree.

1	# Rerere
     2	
     3	With `rerere.enabled` set (`git config --global rerere.enabled true`), git records each manual resolution and reapplies it when the same conflict recurs. Check a reapplied resolution with `git diff` before staging it.

     5	| Command | Purpose |
     6	|---------|---------|
     7	| `git rerere status` | Files with recorded resolutions |
     8	| `git rerere diff` | What rerere would apply |
     9	| `git rerere forget <file>` | Delete a recorded resolution |

     6	
     7	- **Skills**:
     8	  - `actions-monitor`: Watch a PR's CI and stream state events; invokes the logs agent on failures
     9	  - `attach`: Attach an image or video to an issue, PR, comment, or review, through `gh --attach` or the user-attachments endpoint it wraps
    10	  - `copilot`: Cross-model review of the current diff through the Copilot CLI. Slash-invocable only, one call by default and three at most, because the Copilot plan is a fixed budget
    11	  - `notifications`: Inbox management (list, filter, mark read/done, unsubscribe)
    12	  - `pr-comments`: Fetch unresolved review comments from a pull request
    13	  - `stack`: Build, publish, and merge native stacked PRs with the `gh stack` extension
    14	- **Agents**:
    15	  - `github-rulesets-manager`: Configure repository rulesets and branch protection
    16	  - `logs`: Extracts relevant lines from failing-job logs (invoked by `actions-monitor`)
    17	- **Hooks**:
    18	  - Intercepts WebFetch for efficient GitHub data access
    19	  - [`runner-queue.ts`](scripts/runner-queue.ts) follows `gh workflow run` with the new run's place in line when it waits on a self-hosted runner. The model then knows why the run has not started and how long to wait before checking. Silent when the job starts at once or runs on a GitHub-hosted runner. Self-timed to `~/.claude/hook-metrics/github-runner-queue.jsonl`
    20	
    21	    ```text
    22	    [github/runner-queue] Run 39817210542 is queued for a self-hosted runner labeled actions-sandbox: 0 job(s) ahead, 1 matching job(s) running.
    23	    Holding the runner:
    24	    - session-bench run 39815981118 job "bench" on main, started 8m ago (recent successful runs take ~14m)
    25	    ```
    26	- **Mod**: [`register.ts`](mod/register.ts) watches the current branch's pull request and shows its CI and review state at the end of the prompt footer. The model is told when the PR merges or closes, when it conflicts with its base or needs an update that the base requires, when its branch moves to a commit the local repository lacks, when a check newly fails, and when other people review or comment, in one line per author. A conflict alert points at the `git:conflicts` skill and fires even when the conflict is already there as the PR is first seen.
    27	  - **Bot chatter**: a review app's own failing check, named for the app, used to reach the model as a CI failure beside that app's review, and now arrives only as the review. A bot's one-line link, its comments led by a hidden `<!--` marker (summaries edited in place, acknowledgements), and its bodiless thread replies stay out too, judged by shape, with bots known by GitHub's author type. They are logged, not shown. The `reviewers`, `ignore`, and `ignoreBody` options cover the rest.
    28	  - **Whose turn**: the footer used to echo the review decision, and now leads with whom the PR waits on, padded to one width so the glyphs after it hold still: `author`, `agent` while a turn runs, `review`, `merging`, or `ci`. Glyphs with counts follow: failing checks, reviewers waited on, and unresolved threads whose last word is not the session's. Requested changes hold the author's turn until their reviewer is asked again, which a push alone does not do.

Muted chatter sits behind a collapsed row (`m` toggles it), and `r` reads the PR in full at once. Esc or a second `/pr` closes the pane.

     2	name: github:actions-monitor
     3	description: Monitor GitHub Actions runs and extract failure diagnostics. Use when watching PR CI, branch builds, or specific workflow runs.
     4	argument-hint: "[pr-url | branch | run-id] [--max-minutes N] [--interval S]"
     5	effort: low
     6	allowed-tools:
     7	  - Monitor
     8	  - TaskStop
     9	  - Agent
    10	  - Bash(bun:*)
    11	  - Bash(gh run:*)
    12	  - Bash(gh pr view:*)
    13	  - Bash(gh pr checks:*)
    14	  - Bash(git remote:*)
    15	  - Bash(jq:*)
    16	---
    17	
    18	# Actions Monitor
    19	
    20	Watch a PR, branch, or workflow run until it reaches a terminal event, and diagnose each failure. The watch script tracks state and deduplicates events. The monitor is done when the script exits or you stop it with `TaskStop`, with every `failing` event diagnosed along the way.
    21	
    22	## Target
    23	
    24	`$ARGUMENTS` selects the mode:
    25	
    26	- A PR URL selects PR mode. It reads owner and repo from the URL and works from any directory.
    27	- A branch name selects branch mode.
    28	- A run ID selects run-id mode, which covers `workflow_dispatch`, manual triggers, and re-runs.
    29	- With no argument, use the current PR from `gh pr view --json url --jq '.url'`. When the branch has no PR, use branch mode on the current branch.
    30	
    31	Branch and run-id mode read the repo from `git remote get-url origin`. Pass `--repo <owner/repo>` to override it.
    32	
    33	## Start
    34	
    35	Run the script under `Monitor` with `persistent: true` and one mode flag:
    36	
    37	```
    38	bun ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/watch.ts --pr <pr-url>
    39	bun ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/watch.ts --branch <name> [--repo <owner/repo>]
    40	bun ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/watch.ts --run-id <id> [--repo <owner/repo>]
    41	```
    42	
    43	Optional flags are `--interval <seconds>`, `--max-minutes <N>`, `--queued-timeout <minutes>`, and `--api-error-threshold <N>`. Without `--interval`, PR and branch mode derive the interval from recent run durations, and run-id mode polls every 180s.
    44	
    45	## Events
    46	
    47	The script prints one JSON object per line:
    48	
    49	- `{"type":"status","state":"running|failing|success","sha":"...","run_id":"..."}`
    50	- `{"type":"conflicts","sha":"..."}` (PR mode)
    51	- `{"type":"mergeable-unknown","sha":"..."}` (PR mode)
    52	- `{"type":"queued-timeout","minutes":N}`
    53	- `{"type":"api-error","consecutive":N}`
    54	- `{"type":"rate-limited","retry_after":"..."}`
    55	- `{"type":"pr-closed"}` (PR mode, also when the branch is deleted)
    56	- `{"type":"merged"}` (PR mode)
    57	- `{"type":"max-time-reached","minutes":60}`
    58	
    59	The script exits on `status:success`, `pr-closed`, `merged`, and `max-time-reached`. Run-id mode also exits on `status:failing`. PR and branch mode keep watching after `failing`, because a new push or run can follow. A target already green at startup emits one `status:success` and exits.
    60	
    61	## Reactions
    62	
    63	- `failing` with a `run_id`: dispatch the `github:logs` agent with the `run_id` and the PR URL or branch. It returns a JSON summary of the failing jobs and saves the raw logs to a temp path you can read for more detail.
    64	- `failing` with `"run_id": null`: the red check is an external status such as a hosted reviewer or deployment. Name the failing checks from `gh pr checks`.
    65	- `conflicts` and `mergeable-unknown`: report the SHA and leave the response to the caller, such as `pull-request:babysit`. `mergeable-unknown` means GitHub had not settled mergeability after bounded re-polling.
    66	- `queued-timeout` and `api-error`: report them to the user.
    67	- `rate-limited`: wait until `retry_after`, then retry.
    68	
    69	For log parsing, see [references/log-parsing.md](references/log-parsing.md).

1	# Log Parsing
     2	
     3	## CI Log Structure
     4	
     5	CI logs are step-annotated: each step has a start marker and exit code. When a step exits non-zero, the relevant output is between that step's start marker and the exit. GitHub Actions prefixes each line with the step name, so filter to the failing step's lines to discard noise.
     6	
     7	## Narrowing Large Output
     8	
     9	Job logs can be tens of thousands of lines. If per-job output is still too large:
    10	1. Try `--log-failed` to get only failing steps
    11	2. Take the last 100-200 lines. Most tools print a summary section at the end, even with parallel/interleaved output.

1	---
     2	name: github:attach
     3	description: Attach a local image or video to GitHub content so it renders inline in an issue, pull request, comment, or review. Use when attaching a screenshot, recording, or diagram to GitHub content.
     4	allowed-tools:
     5	  - Bash(gh api:*)
     6	  - Bash(gh issue:*)
     7	  - Bash(gh pr:*)
     8	  - Bash(grep:*)
     9	---
    10	
    11	# Attachments
    12	
    13	Images and video in issues and pull requests are served from a user-attachments store. `gh` 2.99.0 added a repeatable `--attach` flag that uploads to it from `gh issue create`, `gh issue edit`, `gh issue comment`, `gh pr create`, `gh pr edit`, and `gh pr comment`. Everything else uploads through the endpoint the flag wraps: review comments and pending reviews, discussions, releases, gists, and any `gh` older than 2.99.0. Both paths exist on GitHub.com and Enterprise Cloud only. Enterprise Server has no attachment store.
    14	
    15	`--attach` on this build: !`gh issue comment --help 2>/dev/null | grep -q -- '--attach' && echo present || echo absent`
    16	
    17	Absent means this `gh` predates 2.99.0. Upgrade it or use the endpoint.
    18	
    19	## The Flag
    20	
    21	Write the body with the local path in the markdown, then name each file on the command. `gh` uploads it and rewrites the reference in place. The image lands where the prose put it. The alt text written in the body wins.
    22	
    23	```bash
    24	gh pr create --title "..." --body-file tmp/pr-body.md --attach ./picker.png --attach ./walkthrough.mp4
    25	```
    26	
    27	- A path is absolute or relative to the directory `gh` runs in.
    28	- A file the body never references is appended to the end, in flag order, with the filename as alt text. Alt text follows the path after `#`: `--attach './picker.png#The wide layout'`.
    29	- `gh pr edit` and `gh issue edit` without a body flag keep the existing body and append.
    30	- Up to 50 files per command.
    31	- When some uploads fail, the issue, pull request, or comment still lands with the ones that succeeded. Its URL prints, and the exit status is non-zero. Read the output before retrying. A blind retry duplicates the assets that already uploaded.
    32	- The token needs write access to the repository.
    33	
    34	## The Endpoint
    35	
    36	`POST https://uploads.github.com/user-attachments/assets` has no REST route and no documentation. `gh api` reaches it by full URL instead. A data-residency Enterprise Cloud tenant has its own upload host in place of `uploads.github.com`. `repository_id` takes the numeric REST id. `gh repo view --json id` returns the GraphQL node id, which fails here.
    37	
    38	```bash
    39	repo_id=$(gh api repos/{owner}/{repo} --jq .id)
    40	
    41	gh api --method POST \
    42	  "https://uploads.github.com/user-attachments/assets?repository_id=$repo_id&name=picker.png&content_type=image/png" \
    43	  --input ./picker.png --jq .url
    44	```
    45	
    46	The response is `{"url": "https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/<uuid>"}`. The token needs write access to that repository. Read-only access also answers 404. That makes a permission problem look like a missing repository.
    47	
    48	An image is ordinary markdown, with `\`, `[`, and `]` escaped in the alt text.
    49	
    50	```markdown
    51	![Wide window](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/<uuid>)
    52	```
    53	
    54	Video has no markdown syntax and no alt text. GitHub renders a player when a bare asset URL is the whole of a paragraph.
    55	
    56	## File Types
    57	
    58	Both paths accept the same list, and nothing outside it uploads. Logs, archives, and PDFs are not supported. On the endpoint, the extension in `name` must agree with `content_type`.
    59	
    60	| Extension | `content_type` |
    61	| --- | --- |
    62	| `.png` | `image/png` |
    63	| `.jpg`, `.jpeg` | `image/jpeg` |
    64	| `.gif` | `image/gif` |
    65	| `.webp` | `image/webp` |
    66	| `.svg` | `image/svg+xml` |
    67	| `.mp4` | `video/mp4` |
    68	| `.mov` | `video/quicktime` |
    69	| `.webm` | `video/webm` |
    70	
    71	Images cap at 10 MB. Video caps at 100 MB on a paid plan and 10 MB on a free one.
    72	
    73	## Irreversibility
    74	
    75	An upload cannot be undone and an asset cannot be deleted. Upload only after the body is final. An unreferenced asset stays stranded permanently. It answers 404 until something references it, unlike the write-access 404 on upload above. A 404 right after uploading does not mean the upload failed.

1	---
     2	name: github:copilot
     3	description: Get a cross-model second opinion on a code change from GPT via the Copilot CLI, then triage what it finds. Use when the ask names GPT, Copilot, a second model, or a cross-model check, and as the cross-model pass on a change that clears the review gate.
     4	argument-hint: "[--base <ref>] [--angles <n>] [--model <name>] [--agentic] [--status] [--dry-run] [--max-bytes <n>] [--force]"
     5	allowed-tools:
     6	  - Bash(bun ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/skills/copilot/scripts/review.ts:*)
     7	  - Bash(git diff:*)
     8	  - Bash(git log:*)
     9	  - Bash(git status:*)
    10	  - Read
    11	  - Grep
    12	  - Glob
    13	  - Edit
    14	---
    15	
    16	# Copilot Review
    17	
    18	A second model, GPT through the Copilot CLI, reviews the diff to catch defects Claude's own review passes miss. The work is done when every finding is triaged and reported as accepted or rejected with a reason.
    19	
    20	## Cost
    21	
    22	The plan grants a fixed monthly credit entitlement that resets on the 1st and does not roll over.
    23	
    24	- A terra call pays about 3.5 credits of fixed prompt overhead before reading any code, about half a median review.
    25	- Output costs 6x input and 60x cache_read.
    26	- Calls don't share a cache. Each angle or spawn re-pays its whole prompt.
    27	- `gpt-5.6-luna` costs a tenth of terra for every token class.
    28	
    29	| model | input | cache_read | cache_write | output |
    30	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    31	| `gpt-5.6-terra` | 200 | 20 | 250 | 1200 |
    32	| `gpt-5.6-luna` | 20 | 2 | 25 | 120 |
    33	
    34	Rates are credits per million tokens, from the CLI's usage ledger.
    35	
    36	## Sizing a Review
    37	
    38	`--status` prints the tier and bands for free. Run it when unsure whether a change qualifies.
    39	
    40	The tier comes from `pace`, credits remaining divided by days to reset: under 25 is constrained, over 60 is abundant, between is normal. The tier sets how strict the gate is. Spend only on changes the gate admits, and leave the rest of the allotment unspent.
    41	
    42	| tier | gate |
    43	| --- | --- |
    44	| constrained | terra only on risk-surface hits, luna one-shot otherwise |
    45	| normal | terra one-shot on gate-worthy changes, skip the rest |
    46	| abundant | terra one-shot on any substantial human change, 3 angles on the risk class, agentic available |
    47	
    48	The bands reuse the Bot Review Gate criteria from the `ship` skill:
    49	
    50	| band | criteria | shape | cost |
    51	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
    52	| skip | bot bumps, prose, lockfiles, reverts, config away from the risk surfaces | none | 0 |
    53	| deep | a runtime surface, auth, sandbox, permissions, secrets, or egress; over ~200 lines or 8 files excluding tests, docs, and lockfiles; a bug `code-review` confirmed; a session that drifted | terra, 1 angle | 7.6-12.4 |
    54	| deep+ | risk-surface hits, abundant tier only | terra, 3 angles | ~22.7 |
    55	| agentic | destructive, concurrent, or auth changes, abundant tier only | capped session | up to 60 |
    56	
    57	The script enforces the hard stops. It refuses `--agentic` outside the abundant tier, degrades to luna below 150 credits remaining, refuses a run whose session cap could reach billed overage, and stops when it cannot read the meter. It reads the meter once with no lock, so run one review at a time.
    58	
    59	## Run It
    60	
    61	```bash
    62	bun ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/skills/copilot/scripts/review.ts [--base <ref>] [--angles <n>] [--model <name>]
    63	```
    64	
    65	The script resolves the diff, inlines the changed files, and prints each angle's findings with credits spent and remaining.
    66	
    67	- `--base <ref>`: diff base. Defaults to the upstream tracking ref, then `origin/main`.
    68	- `--angles <1-3>`: independent calls over disjoint defect classes. Defaults to 1.
    69	- `--model <name>`: defaults to `gpt-5.6-terra`.
    70	- `--agentic`: one capped tool-using session. Refuses `--angles` above 1.
    71	- `--status`: print tier and bands, free.
    72	- `--dry-run`: print the assembled prompts and their size, free.
    73	- `--max-bytes <n>`: move the 120 KB prompt cap, a spend guard.
    74	- `--force`: run past the cap. Narrow with `--base` first, then `--max-bytes`.
    75	
    76	#### Angles
    77	
    78	| angles | coverage |
    79	| --- | --- |
    80	| 1 | every class, one call |
    81	| 2 | unchecked failure and correctness, then data loss and security |
    82	| 3 | adds contracts, concurrency, and resources |
    83	
    84	Use 3 only for security-sensitive, destructive, or concurrent changes in the abundant tier.
    85	
    86	#### Agentic Mode
    87	
    88	`--agentic` gives Copilot a throwaway `git worktree` at HEAD with tools. It reads callers, tests, and history. It runs under a 60-credit cap, several times a one-shot's cost. It needs a clean tree. Otherwise the worktree differs from the diff. Use it only on changes you authored. Review a diff containing untrusted third-party text as a one-shot, which runs without tools.
    89	
    90	#### Models
    91	
    92	`copilot help config` lists the model names the CLI accepts. A listed name can still return "not available" on this account, and a rejected probe is free because the CLI fails before inference. The GPT-5.6 family is `sol`, `terra`, and `luna`, and `sol` is not reachable on this plan.
    93	
    94	## Triage the Findings
    95	
    96	A one-shot run has no tools and sees only the inlined text, so treat each finding as a review-bot claim. Read the actual code for each one:
    97	
    98	- Real: fix it, or state why you are deferring.
    99	- Wrong: state what the model missed, often a caller or invariant outside the inlined text.
   100	- Unsure: put it to the user.
   101	
   102	Report accepted and rejected findings, each with its reason. Settle a rejected finding yourself rather than re-running for another opinion.
   103	
   104	## Gotchas
   105	
   106	#### Sandbox, `HOME`, and Auth
   107	
   108	The script points `HOME` at `~/.cache/claude/copilot-home`, because the sandbox blocks writes to `~/.copilot` (`I/O error: Operation not permitted (os error 1)`). Keep the sandbox on. That home persists. Read the spend ledger there afterward, and resume a session with `--resume`. `--no-custom-instructions` keeps repo instructions out of the review.
   109	
   110	The redirect hides Copilot's own logins and `gh`'s. When none of `COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN`, `GH_TOKEN`, or `GITHUB_TOKEN` is set, the script runs `gh auth token` under the real `HOME` and passes it as `COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN`. When no token resolves, it refuses before spending. Fix that with `gh auth login` or by exporting one of the three variables.
   111	
   112	`user/settings.json` allows `api.individual.githubcopilot.com`. A `Failed to load models` with a `tunnel error` means the login uses a different Copilot host, such as a Business plan's. Grant that exact host there.
   113	
   114	#### What Reaches GitHub
   115	
   116	The diff and full changed files go to GitHub with no redaction, including untracked files from `git ls-files --others --exclude-standard`. The script skips symlinks that point out of the repository. Check the diff for secrets and fixtures before reviewing a change that touches them.
   117	
   118	#### Agentic Containment
   119	
   120	Agentic mode passes `--allow-all-tools` minus `--deny-tool write`, `--deny-tool url`, `shell(git push)`, `shell(gh:*)`, `shell(curl:*)`, and `shell(wget:*)`. It contains misbehavior. A deliberate attacker can get past it.
   121	
   122	- Shell redirection can still write. The disposable worktree is the write barrier.
   123	- The worktree shares the parent's `.git`. `git update-ref` and `git config` reach the real repository. The reflog records ref moves.
   124	- Deny matching works on first-level subcommand grammar. An exotic invocation could reach `git push`.
   125	- Prompt injection in the diff gets past every flag. Running agentic mode only on your own changes covers it.
   126	
   127	#### Overage
   128	
   129	A separate `$0` stop-usage budget on All AI Credit SKUs blocks billed overage, even though the plan reports `overage_permitted: true` with a 2000-credit overage entitlement.
   130	
   131	#### Review Prompt
   132	
   133	The script's prompt lists the defect classes in priority order and tells the model to skip summarizing the change. Keep both when editing it.

     2	name: github:pr-comments
     3	description: Fetch, reply to, and resolve review threads on a GitHub pull request. Use when checking what review feedback needs addressing, whether threads are resolved, replying to review comments, or clearing AI-reviewer threads after acting on them.
     4	argument-hint: "<pr-url> [--role author|reviewer] [--bots] [--include-resolved]"
     5	allowed-tools:
     6	  ["Bash(bun ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/pr-comments.ts:*)", "Bash(bun ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/review-threads.ts:*)"]
     7	---
     8	
     9	# PR Review Comments
    10	
    11	## Fetching
    12	
    13	```bash
    14	bun ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/pr-comments.ts <pr-url> [--role author|reviewer] [--since last-review|<date>] [--bots] [--include-resolved]
    15	```
    16	
    17	Output is markdown grouped by file, with each thread's node `id` for replying and resolving. Resolved threads are excluded by default. Outdated threads are included and marked.
    18	
    19	- `--role`: `author` fetches all unresolved threads. `reviewer` fetches unresolved threads the authenticated user started. Defaults by whether the authenticated user is the PR author.
    20	- `--since last-review`: threads with activity since the last relevant review. As author, that is the latest review by a human other than you. As reviewer, it is your latest submitted review. An ISO date (`2025-01-15`) sets an explicit cutoff.
    21	- `--bots`: only review-bot threads, meaning accounts the API types as `Bot` plus the plugin's configured reviewers. Pass `--reviewers=${user_config.reviewers}` with it. Identify bots through this filter.
    22	- `--include-resolved`: include resolved threads, tagged `(resolved)`, to find threads resolved without a reply.
    23	
    24	## Replying and Resolving
    25	
    26	```bash
    27	bun ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/review-threads.ts reply <thread-id> [--resolve] --body "..."
    28	bun ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/review-threads.ts react <thread-id> [--down] [--resolve]
    29	bun ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/review-threads.ts resolve <thread-id>
    30	```
    31	
    32	`reply` also takes `--bodyFile <path>` or stdin. Upload a screenshot for a reply through the endpoint in `github:attach`, since `gh`'s `--attach` does not reach review threads.
    33	
    34	Resolve each thread together with a reply or a reaction, through `reply --resolve` or `react --resolve`. The reply or reaction records why the thread closed. React with a thumbs up where an acknowledgment reply would add nothing (test coverage, a rename, an obvious guard). The reaction goes on the thread's first comment.
    35	
    36	`--down` is feedback to a bot reviewer whose comment was wrong or unhelpful. Use it only on bot threads and only in an attended run.
    37	
    38	On bot threads, push the fix and resolve, or react with a thumbs up. When a reply is needed, write it as a terse note for a future human reader ("Guarded with a null check").

1	---
     2	name: github:stack
     3	description: Publish and merge GitHub native stacked pull requests with the `gh stack` extension. Use when a branch is stacked on another branch rather than the default branch, when linking a chain of branches into a stack on GitHub, or when merging a PR that belongs to a stack. Load before running any `gh stack` command.
     4	allowed-tools:
     5	  - Bash(gh stack:*)
     6	  - Bash(gh pr:*)
     7	  - Bash(gh api:*)
     8	---
     9	
    10	# Stacked Pull Requests
    11	
    12	`gh stack` (the `github/gh-stack` extension) drives GitHub's native stacked PRs. The stack object on GitHub and the merge are the same under either layout below. The layout decides how the stack gets built and published.
    13	
    14	## Layouts
    15	
    16	**Native tracking** keeps every layer checked out in one working tree. `gh stack` owns the branches, the rebases, and the publish, with the interactive PR editor, cascading rebase, and one-command sync.
    17	
    18	**External tracking** keeps each layer somewhere else, typically its own worktree. Another tool owns the rebases and `gh stack link` publishes the result without writing local state.
    19	
    20	Pick per stack. Native tracking fits a stack you are actively reshaping, where reordering and folding layers matters more than working two layers at once. External tracking fits a stack whose layers are worked on in parallel or over a long stretch, where each layer wants its own checkout, editor, and running services.
    21	
    22	Read the current state with `gh stack view --short` (add `--json` to parse it). It answers from local tracking. Output means native tracking, and an error means the stack is not tracked in this clone. A stack published by `link` exists on GitHub and is still absent from `view`.
    23	
    24	Keep each stack under one layout. The local-tracking commands silently under-perform against branches they can't check out. `gh stack rebase` prints `✓ Rebased <branch>` and changes nothing when that branch is checked out in a different worktree ([gh-stack#35](https://github.com/github/gh-stack/issues/35)).
    25	
    26	Exit code 9 means the repository doesn't have stacked PRs enabled. Code 6 means a branch belongs to more than one stack, or more than one remote is configured with no `remote.pushDefault` set. `link`, `submit`, `push`, and `sync` take `--remote` for that second case.
    27	
    28	Stack numbers and PR numbers share one sequence per repository, so a bare number is unambiguous wherever a command takes either.
    29	
    30	## Detection
    31	
    32	Stack membership lives on the API. Given a PR number, this query answers under either layout with nothing checked out.
    33	
    34	```bash
    35	gh api graphql -f query='query($owner:String!,$repo:String!,$number:Int!){repository(owner:$owner,name:$repo){pullRequest(number:$number){stack{number size}}}}' \
    36	  -F owner=<owner> -F repo=<repo> -F number=<n>
    37	```
    38	
    39	`"stack": null` means the PR isn't stacked. Otherwise `number` is the stack number and `size` its PR count. `gh pr view` has no stack field.
    40	
    41	To read the other layers, ask for the entries. `position` counts up from the base, so position 1 is the bottom.
    42	
    43	```bash
    44	gh api graphql -f query='query($owner:String!,$repo:String!,$number:Int!){repository(owner:$owner,name:$repo){pullRequest(number:$number){stackEntry{position stack{entries(first:50){nodes{position pullRequest{number state isDraft reviewDecision mergeStateStatus}}}}}}}}' \
    45	  -F owner=<owner> -F repo=<repo> -F number=<n>
    46	```
    47	
    48	There is no CI field here. `mergeStateStatus` is the proxy. `CLEAN` is mergeable with checks passing. `BLOCKED` is blocked by a rule or a missing review, `UNSTABLE` is a non-passing commit status, `DIRTY` is a conflict, and `BEHIND` is a stale head ref.
    49	
    50	## Native Tracking
    51	
    52	Build the stack with `init` and `add`. `init` adopts branches that exist and creates the ones that don't, bottom to top.
    53	
    54	```bash
    55	gh stack init auth-layer api-routes ui-components  # adopt or create a whole stack
    56	gh stack init --base develop my-feature            # non-default trunk
    57	gh stack add -Am "Add rate limiting" rate-limits   # new layer on top, committing staged work
    58	```
    59	
    60	`gh stack submit` pushes every branch, opens the missing PRs, fixes the bases, and creates or updates the stack object. Interactively it opens a single-screen editor to write each new PR's title, description, and draft state before submitting them together. Use it whenever the bodies matter.
    61	
    62	Non-interactively, and with `--auto`, it skips the editor and auto-generates titles. It also creates new PRs as **drafts**. Pass `--open` to get PRs that are ready for review.
    63	
    64	`gh stack sync` is the maintenance command: fetch, reconcile against the stack on GitHub, fast-forward the trunk, cascade-rebase each branch onto its parent, push atomically with `--force-with-lease`, and link the open PRs into a stack once two exist. It never opens PRs. `--prune` deletes local branches for merged PRs, which is the cleanup after a stack lands.
    65	
    66	Use the narrower commands when sync is too much: `gh stack rebase` for the cascading rebase alone (`--downstack`, `--upstack`, `--no-trunk`, and `--continue` / `--abort` around conflicts), and `gh stack push` to push without rebasing. `push` is per-branch and not atomic. A rejected branch leaves the ones before it already updated.
    67	
    68	`gh stack modify` restructures the stack interactively: drop, fold, insert, reorder, rename. Run `submit` afterward, since it changes local branches and leaves GitHub behind.
    69	
    70	Move around with `gh stack checkout` (bare, for a picker over local and remote stacks), plus `up`, `down`, `top`, `bottom`, `trunk`, and `switch`.
    71	
    72	## External Tracking
    73	
    74	Let the other tool rebase and push the whole stack first. `link` pushes without force. It rejects a branch whose remote copy has diverged, which is every branch immediately after a rebase.
    75	
    76	`gh stack link` takes branches, PR numbers, or PR URLs bottom to top. It pushes each branch, opens a PR for any branch missing one, corrects the base of any PR whose base breaks the chain, and creates or updates the stack object.
    77	
    78	```bash
    79	gh stack link auth-layer api-routes ui-components   # create or update a stack
    80	gh stack link 7 ui-polish                           # append to stack 7
    81	gh stack link --base develop auth-layer api-routes  # non-default trunk
    82	```
    83	
    84	It needs at least two arguments, or a stack number plus what to append, and only ever adds to a stack. `--open` marks new and existing PRs ready for review.
    85	
    86	Open the PR yourself with `gh pr create --base <parent>` before linking whenever the title and body matter. `link` reuses an open PR when it finds one, and auto-generates a title from the commit subject or branch name for the ones it creates. `link` has no editor.
    87	
    88	## Merging
    89	
    90	`gh pr merge` does not work on a stacked PR. Use `gh stack merge`, which takes a stack number or a PR number, never a URL, and works under either layout.
    91	
    92	```bash
    93	gh stack merge 42 --yes --<method>  # everything up to and including PR #42
    94	gh stack merge 7 --yes --<method>   # stack 7, no local checkout needed
    95	```
    96	
    97	`--yes` runs it headlessly. Name the method rather than inheriting the default, which is whichever one you used last, and take it from the repo (`gh repo view --json squashMergeAllowed,mergeCommitAllowed,rebaseMergeAllowed`). Always pass a number, so the merge target does not depend on the current branch.
    98	
    99	The merge is all-or-nothing across every PR at or below the target. One layer that can't merge sinks the call, and the reason comes back on stderr. Layers above stay open, and GitHub retargets and rebases them onto the new base. Pull that down afterward (`gh stack sync` under native tracking, the external tool otherwise), because every open layer is stale locally until you do.
   100	
   101	Only open-and-not-draft state is checked before submitting. GitHub evaluates branch protection and repository rules when the merge runs, and those requirements can't be bypassed for a stack.
   102	
   103	When the base branch uses a merge queue, the stack goes on the queue instead of merging directly. The queue picks the method and ignores any method flag with a warning, and the PRs enter together but land as the queue processes them, possibly in separate groups.
   104	
   105	## Switching Layouts
   106	
   107	`gh stack checkout <stack-number>` adopts a stack that exists only on GitHub: it queries the API, fetches the branches, and sets up local tracking. This is how a stack published by `link` becomes natively tracked, and it wants a working tree the branches can all be checked out in.
   108	
   109	`gh stack unstack --local` drops local tracking and leaves the stack on GitHub, which is the reverse. Without `--local`, `unstack` also unstacks on GitHub, and takes a stack number to do that from anywhere. GitHub keeps PRs stacked when they are queued or have auto-merge enabled.

1	# GitLab Plugin
     2	
     3	GitLab workflow best practices and glab CLI usage for Claude Code.
     4	
     5	## Contents
     6	
     7	### Skills
     8	
     9	- The `merge-request` skill covers working with merge requests
    10	- The `ci-monitor` skill watches an MR's CI and streams state events, invoking the logs agent on failures. It also covers `.gitlab-ci.yml` authoring and linting
    11	- The `api` skill provides REST and GraphQL API access, plus GitLab docs navigation
    12	
    13	### Agents
    14	
    15	- The `logs` agent extracts relevant lines from failing-job logs and is invoked by `ci-monitor`
    16	
    17	### Hooks
    18	
    19	- Transforms GitLab URLs into API requests for better content fetching
    20	- Detects glab OAuth token expiration and provides recovery guidance
    21	- Denies gh-isms that always fail against GitLab (`glab api --jq`, `gh pr` on a GitLab remote, escaped-`$` inline GraphQL, hallucinated mutations, an `@<file>` body glab would post as the bare path) with the corrected form, and nudges loading `gitlab:merge-request` before hand-rolled MR transactions
    22	
    23	### Mod
    24	
    25	- [`register.ts`](mod/register.ts) watches the current branch's merge request and shows its pipeline and approval state at the end of the prompt footer. The model is told when the MR merges or closes, when it conflicts with its target or needs a rebase that the target requires, when its branch moves to a commit the local repository lacks, when a job newly fails, when changes are requested, and when other people approve, revoke an approval, or comment, in one line per author. A conflict alert points at the `git:conflicts` skill and fires even when the conflict is already there as the MR is first seen.
    26	  - **Bot chatter**: a bot's one-line link and its notes led by a hidden `<!--` marker (summaries edited in place, acknowledgements) used to reach the model as comments, and now stay out, judged by shape. A bot's diff note still arrives as a finding. GitLab notes carry no bot flag, so bots are service accounts by name plus the `reviewers` option. Muted notes are logged, not shown, and the `ignore` and `ignoreBody` options mute more.
    27	  - **Whose turn**: the footer used to echo the merge status, and now leads with whom the MR waits on, padded to one width so the glyphs after it hold still: `author`, `agent` while a turn runs, `review`, `merging`, or `ci`. Glyphs with counts follow: failing jobs, reviewers waited on, approvals nobody was asked for, and unresolved threads whose last word is not the session's. A request for changes holds the author's turn until its reviewer is asked again.
    28	  - **Merging**: auto-merge and a merge train show as `merging` with the train position. Leaving the train or auto-merge without merging wakes the model.
    29	  - **Pane**: `/mr` opens a pane with the MR title as a link, the footer status in color, then jobs (failing and running ones listed, passing ones counted), review, merge state, and when it polled and polls next. Muted chatter sits behind a collapsed row (`m` toggles it), and `r` reads the MR in full at once. Esc or a second `/mr` closes the pane.
    30	  - **Polling**: a timer chain used to poll every 1 to 10 minutes forever, and one lost timer ended the watch. A wall-clock ticker now runs an overdue poll on the first tick after a wake, backs off to every two hours while nothing changes, and returns to minutes on a change or a turn. Approvals, notes, and jobs are reused while the MR's `updated_at` and pipeline hold.
    31	  - Every decision, send, muted item, turn change, backoff, and late or revived poll is logged to `mod-events`. Needs a signed-in `glab`. Set the `watch` option to false to turn it off

1	---
     2	name: gitlab:api
     3	description: GitLab REST and GraphQL API access via glab. Use when making API requests, running GraphQL queries or mutations, querying project data, automating GitLab operations, or looking up GitLab feature, API, or CI/CD documentation.
     4	---
     5	# GitLab API
     6	
     7	REST and GraphQL API access via `glab api`.
     8	
     9	## Placeholders
    10	
    11	Auto-resolve to current project values:
    12	
    13	- `:fullpath` - Full project path (e.g., `group/project`)
    14	- `:id` - Project ID
    15	- `:branch` - Current branch
    16	- `:user` / `:username` - Current user
    17	
    18	```bash
    19	glab api projects/:fullpath/merge_requests
    20	```
    21	
    22	## REST
    23	
    24	```bash
    25	glab api projects/:id/issues                          # GET
    26	glab api projects/:id/issues -X POST -f title="..."   # POST with field
    27	glab api projects/:id/issues --paginate               # All pages
    28	```
    29	
    30	#### No `--jq`/`-q`
    31	
    32	Output filtering flags belong to `gh api`. Pipe to `jq` instead: `glab api <endpoint> | jq '<filter>'`. There is also no `--json` flag anywhere in `glab`. Use `--output json`.
    33	
    34	#### Error Bodies Land on Stdout
    35	
    36	A 404/4xx response is a JSON error body (`{"message":"404 Not found"}`), so `glab api ... | jq '.field'` turns the real HTTP error into misleading `null` output or a jq type error (`Cannot index string`, `Cannot iterate over object`). When a pipeline misbehaves, rerun the `glab api` call bare and read the body before touching the jq filter.
    37	
    38	#### Pagination Pitfall
    39	
    40	`--paginate` concatenates JSON arrays across pages as `][`, producing invalid JSON (e.g., `[{...}][{...}]`). Fix by replacing `][` with `,` before parsing: `.replace(/\]\s*\[/g, ",")`.
    41	
    42	#### Nested Fields
    43	
    44	`-f` and `--raw-field` silently drop bracket-nested keys like `position[base_sha]=...`. For nested objects, write JSON to a file and use `--input`:
    45	
    46	```bash
    47	echo '{"position":{"base_sha":"abc","head_sha":"def","old_path":"file.ts","new_path":"file.ts","position_type":"text","new_line":10}}' > /tmp/payload.json
    48	glab api projects/:id/merge_requests/:iid/discussions -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" --input /tmp/payload.json
    49	```
    50	
    51	## Uploads
    52	
    53	An image or video for an MR or issue body goes through project uploads, which take multipart form data. `--form` sends the file. `-F` reads the file and embeds its bytes in a JSON body field, which the endpoint rejects with HTTP 400.
    54	
    55	```bash
    56	glab api projects/:id/uploads --form "file=@./shot.png" | jq -r .markdown
    57	```
    58	
    59	The response carries `url` (a project-relative `/uploads/<hash>/shot.png`) and `markdown` (`![shot](/uploads/<hash>/shot.png)`). Paste the markdown into the description or note. The relative URL renders anywhere inside that project. `glab mr` and `glab issue` have no attach flag. The upload runs before the create or update.
    60	
    61	## GraphQL
    62	
    63	```bash
    64	glab api graphql -f query='{ currentUser { username } }'
    65	```
    66	
    67	For pagination, accept `$endCursor` variable and fetch `pageInfo { hasNextPage, endCursor }`.
    68	
    69	#### Queries With Variables: Use a Quoted Heredoc
    70	
    71	Escaping `$` in an inline `-f query='mutation($var...)'` corrupts the query (GitLab returns `Expected VAR_SIGN, actual: UNKNOWN_CHAR`). A quoted heredoc needs no escaping:
    72	
    73	```bash
    74	glab api graphql -f query="$(cat <<'GQL'
    75	mutation($projectPath: ID!, $iid: String!, $userId: UserID!) {
    76	  mergeRequestReviewerRereview(input: { projectPath: $projectPath, iid: $iid, userId: $userId }) { errors }
    77	}
    78	GQL
    79	)" -f projectPath=group/project -f iid=123 -f userId="gid://gitlab/User/42"
    80	```
    81	
    82	Pass variables with `-f` (strings), not `-F`: `-F` coerces numeric-looking values to int, and `iid` is typed `String!`. `projectPath` is typed `ID!`, not `String!`.
    83	
    84	#### Hallucinated Mutations
    85	
    86	Do not guess mutation names from GitHub's schema. `mergeRequestSetAutoMerge` and `mergeRequestRequestReview` are not in GitLab's schema. Auto-merge is REST-only (`glab mr merge --auto-merge`, or the `gitlab:merge-request` skill's `merge.ts` for merge trains). Re-requesting review is `mergeRequestReviewerRereview`. Requesting changes is `mergeRequestRequestChanges`. Trial-executing a guessed mutation runs it for real if it exists, so use documented forms only.
    87	
    88	## Output
    89	
    90	- `--output json` (default) - Pretty-printed JSON
    91	- `--output ndjson` - Newline-delimited, works with `jq` streaming
    92	
    93	## Documentation
    94	
    95	For `glab` command reference, use `glab <command> --help` instead of web docs (the `/cli/` pages duplicate CLI help output). For everything else, [GitLab docs](https://docs.gitlab.com/) paths:
    96	
    97	| Need | Path |
    98	|------|------|
    99	| REST endpoints | `/api/` |
   100	| MR API fields | `/api/merge_requests/` |
   101	| GraphQL schema | `/api/graphql/reference/` |
   102	| CI/CD YAML syntax | `/ci/yaml/` |
   103	| Predefined CI variables | `/ci/variables/` |
   104	| Feature concepts | `/topics/` |
   105	| UI configuration | `/user/` |
   106	| Self-managed admin | `/administration/` |

     3	description: Watch GitLab CI and investigate pipeline failures. Use when a pipeline or job is failing or red, when watching MR CI, branch builds, or a specific pipeline, when waiting for CI to go green, or when authoring or validating .gitlab-ci.yml.
     4	argument-hint: "[mr-url | branch | pipeline-id] [--max-minutes N] [--project group/project]"
     5	effort: low
     6	allowed-tools:
     7	  - Monitor
     8	  - TaskStop

    16	---
    17	
    18	# CI Monitor
    19	
    20	Watch a GitLab pipeline and report its outcome to the caller: green, a failure diagnosis, or the event that ended the watch. Done when the watcher has exited or been stopped and the outcome is reported.
    21	
    22	## Target
    23	
    24	$ARGUMENTS
    25	
    26	- MR URL (`https://gitlab.com/group/project/-/merge_requests/123`): `--mr <url>`
    27	- Branch name: `--branch <name>`
    28	- Pipeline ID: `--pipeline-id <id>`
    29	- No argument: use the current branch's MR from `glab mr view --output json | jq -r '.web_url'`.
    30	
    31	Branch and pipeline-id modes infer the project from the git remote. Pass `--project <group/project>` to override.
    32	
    33	## Watch
    34	
    35	Run the watcher with the `Monitor` tool and `persistent: true`:
    36	
    37	```bash
    38	bun ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/watch.ts --mr <url> | --branch <name> | --pipeline-id <id> [--project <group/project>]
    39	```
    40	
    41	Optional flags: `--interval <seconds>`, `--max-minutes <N>`, `--queued-timeout <minutes>`, `--api-error-threshold <N>`.
    42	
    43	The watcher ignores `external` and `parent_pipeline` pipelines. A `success` is confirmed against the pipeline's jobs, so a pipeline reporting success with a failed required job reports `failing`. A pipeline whose jobs cannot be read keeps polling and surfaces as `api-error` if it persists.
    44	
    45	## Events
    46	
    47	The script prints one JSON object per line. `run_id` is the GitLab pipeline ID.
    48	
    49	| Event | Meaning | Watcher exits | Action |
    50	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
    51	| `{"type":"status","state":"running"}` | Pipeline in progress | no | Keep watching |
    52	| `{"type":"status","state":"failing"}` | A job failed | pipeline-id mode only | Dispatch `gitlab:logs` (below) and report its summary |
    53	| `{"type":"status","state":"success"}` | Green, job-confirmed | yes | Report green |
    54	| `{"type":"conflicts","sha":"..."}` | MR conflicts with target | no | Report the SHA and stop the monitor |
    55	| `{"type":"mergeable-unknown","sha":"..."}` | Merge status unsettled | no | Report the SHA |
    56	| `{"type":"queued-timeout","minutes":N}` | Queued past threshold | no | Report once |
    57	| `{"type":"api-error","consecutive":N}` | `glab` failures crossed threshold | no | Report once; stop the monitor if it repeats |
    58	| `{"type":"rate-limited","retry_after":"..."}` | `glab` rate limit | no | Report once; stop the monitor if it repeats |
    59	| `{"type":"merged"}` | MR merged | yes | Report |
    60	| `{"type":"pr-closed"}` | MR closed unmerged or source branch deleted | yes | Report |
    61	| `{"type":"max-time-reached","minutes":N}` | Wall-clock cap | yes | Report |
    62	
    63	`conflicts`, `mergeable-unknown`, `merged`, and `pr-closed` occur in MR mode only.
    64	
    65	On `failing`, pass `run_id` to the logs agent:
    66	
    67	```
    68	Agent(subagent_type="gitlab:logs", prompt="Fetch failing-job logs for pipeline <run_id>. Return the JSON summary described in the logs agent definition.")
    69	```
    70	
    71	Report the diagnosis and leave fixes, conflict resolution, and merge checks to the caller (`pull-request:babysit` owns fixes). Stop a running watcher with `TaskStop`.
    72	
    73	## Config Authoring
    74	
    75	For editing `.gitlab-ci.yml` rather than watching a run:
    76	
    77	```bash
    78	glab ci lint               # Validate .gitlab-ci.yml before pushing
    79	glab ci status             # Pipeline status for current branch
    80	glab ci list               # List recent pipelines
    81	glab ci run                # Trigger a pipeline for the current branch
    82	glab ci view               # Interactive pipeline/job view
    83	glab ci trace <job-id>     # Stream job logs
    84	glab ci retry <job-id>     # Retry a failed job
    85	```
    86	
    87	Keyword syntax is at <https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/yaml/> and predefined variables at <https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/variables/>.

     2	name: gitlab:merge-request
     3	description: Working with GitLab merge requests via glab. Use when creating, updating, reviewing, or merging MRs, enabling auto-merge or merge trains, requesting or re-requesting reviewers, handling approvals, or working review threads, discussions, and draft notes. Load before running any `glab mr` or MR-mutating `glab api` command.
     4	argument-hint: "[create | merge | review | discussions | block] [--draft] [--auto] [--role author|reviewer]"
     5	allowed-tools:
     6	  - Bash(bun ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/*:*)
