    10	---
    11	# Merge Requests
    12	
    13	Scripts directory (absolute, for invocations from other skills where `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` points elsewhere): !`mkdir -p /tmp/claude/gitlab-skill 2>/dev/null; touch "/tmp/claude/gitlab-skill/${CLAUDE_SESSION_ID}" 2>/dev/null; echo "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts"`
    14	
    15	## Arguments
    16	
    17	`$0` (optional verb) routes to a section below. With no verb, infer the operation from the request.
    18	
    19	- `create`: open an MR, see [Creating](#creating). `--draft` opens it as a draft.
    20	- `merge`: see [Merging](#merging). `--auto` enables auto-merge (`merge.ts --auto-merge`).
    21	- `review`: see [Reviews](#reviews). `--role reviewer` (default) fetches MRs awaiting your review. `--role author` triages threads on MRs you authored.
    22	- `discussions`: see [Discussions](#discussions).
    23	- `block`: block an MR until another merges, see [blocking.md](blocking.md).
    24	
    25	## Merging
    26	
    27	Merge only through `merge.ts`. It handles merge trains, auto-merge, and squash. A bare `glab mr merge` turns on auto-merge whenever a pipeline is running. The MR then merges later instead of now. `merge.ts` always sends `--auto-merge=<choice>`.
    28	
    29	```bash
    30	bun ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/merge.ts
    31	bun ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/merge.ts feature-branch --auto-merge --squash
    32	bun ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/merge.ts feature-branch --status
    33	```
    34	
    35	`--status` prints merge readiness as JSON without mutating the MR: target branch, draft state, `detailed_merge_status`, head pipeline, and `rebased_on_target`, an ancestry check computed from git. Trust `rebased_on_target` over the API's conflict fields, which lag.
    36	
    37	#### Re-Arm After a Push
    38	
    39	A push cancels queued auto-merge and drops the MR from the merge train. Re-run `merge.ts --auto-merge` after every push to an MR meant to auto-merge. It is idempotent and retries through the `approvals_syncing` window after a push. When `reset_approvals_on_push` is on, also [re-request reviewers](#re-request-reviewers) in the same pass.
    40	
    41	To inspect the active train or clear a stuck entry, see [merge-trains.md](merge-trains.md).
    42	
    43	## Stacked MRs
    44	
    45	Merging one layer of a stack leaves the layer above it targeting the merged branch, and GitLab does not retarget it. After every layer merges, retarget, rebase, and verify the next one per [stacked-mrs.md](stacked-mrs.md).
    46	
    47	## Creating
    48	
    49	- Push the branch first: `git push -u origin feature-branch && glab mr create --fill`.
    50	- `--fill` populates title and description from commits and cannot combine with `--title`/`--description`.
    51	- Pass a body with `--description-file file.md` (gh's `--body-file` does not exist here) in place of `--description "$(cat file.md)"`, which passes the body through the shell and keeps it out of some hooks.
    52	- `glab mr` has no attach flag. Upload screenshots through project uploads per `gitlab:api` and paste the returned markdown into the description.
    53	- `--reviewer` and `--assignee` silently drop unknown usernames. Resolve exact usernames first, then confirm they appear in `glab mr view`:
    54	
    55	```bash
    56	glab api projects/:id/members/all --paginate | jq '.[] | select(.name | test("<name>"; "i")) | {name, username}'
    57	```
    58	
    59	## Reviews
    60	
    61	Review feedback goes out as draft notes published together, per [review.md](review.md), which also covers the review base, code suggestions, and approvals.
    62	
    63	`review-queue.ts` lists MRs awaiting your first review across all projects as `[{ url, reference, title }]`:
    64	
    65	```bash
    66	bun ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/review-queue.ts
    67	```
    68	
    69	For the underlying GraphQL, reading review state, and grouping every review-requested MR by next actor, see [review-state.md](review-state.md).
    70	
    71	## Re-Request Reviewers
    72	
    73	After a push resets approvals, the `mergeRequestReviewerRereview` mutation sets an assigned reviewer's `reviewState` back to `UNREVIEWED`. See [Re-Request Review](review-state.md#re-request-review) for the user-ID lookup and exact mutation.
    74	
    75	## Discussions
    76	
    77	```bash
    78	# Open threads, one line each
    79	bun ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/discussions.ts list <iid> --resolvable --unresolved --format digest
    80	
    81	# Only review-bot threads
    82	bun ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/discussions.ts list <iid> --bots --reviewers=${user_config.reviewers}
    83	
    84	bun ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/discussions.ts resolve <iid> <discussion-id>...
    85	```
    86	
    87	See [discussions.md](discussions.md) for the other commands, the JSON schema, and API pitfalls.

     8	
     9	## Arguments
    10	
    11	Parse `$ARGUMENTS`:
    12	
    13	- `--type bug|feature|refactor|spike`: use that type's guide. Default: infer the type per [Issue Types](#issue-types).
    14	- `--compact`: write the trivial body per [Section Selection](#section-selection), still with frontmatter. Default: size the body to the issue.
    15	
    16	## Issue Types
    17	
    18	| Type | When to Use | Guide |
    19	|------|-------------|-------|
    20	| Bug | Something is broken | `bug.md` |
    21	| Feature | New capability | `feature.md` |
    22	| Refactor | Internal improvement, no behavior change | `refactor.md` |
    23	| Spike | Timeboxed investigation; output is a recommendation, not a shipped change | `spike.md` |
    24	
    25	## Workflow
    26	
    27	Read the type guide, gather context from code and related issues, and draft the refinement. Write it to `tmp/issue-<slug>.md` and output it for approval. After approval, hand the file to the platform skill (for Linear, `linear:linear`), which owns all save mechanics, including mapping frontmatter to tracker fields. On GitHub, a screenshot the body references by local path goes on `gh issue create --attach`, per `github:attach`.
    28	
    29	## Output Structure
    30	
    31	YAML frontmatter for the metadata a tracker stores as fields, then the body below the closing `---`. The body leads with the summary prose directly, under no heading.
    32	
    33	```markdown
    34	---
    35	title: fix connection pool exhaustion under load   # sentence case, one line, no long parentheticals
    36	type: bug                                           # bug | feature | refactor | spike
    37	labels: [performance, database]                     # optional; neutral tags
    38	priority: high                                      # optional; urgent | high | medium | low
    39	relations:                                          # optional; tracker links per relation
    40	  blocks: []
    41	  blocked-by: []
    42	  related:
    43	    - https://linear.app/acme/issue/ENG-1970

    48	time out, so downstream jobs read a partial snapshot as if it were complete.
    49

    51	
    52	## 🤖 Agent Context
    53	```

    56	
    57	A related issue you found belongs under `relations` as a tracker link, kept out of the body. Mention another issue in the body only when it tells the reader something the relation can't: what a prior attempt tried, why upstream work matters. The body has no Related Issues section. Link a source the body relies on (an RFC, a status page, an API reference) inline in the sentence that relies on it.
    58	
    59	## Section Selection
    60	
    61	Keep a section only when it tells the reader something they couldn't have guessed. Cut sections whose content is tautological ("tests must pass"), template residue ("no behavior change"), or obvious given the issue's size.
    62	
    63	For a substantial issue, the opening summary plus one type section is the floor. Grow only when content demands. A trivial issue needs none of that frame: a sentence or two that names the problem and points at the code is enough.
    64	
    65	## Agent Context
    66	
    67	What you learned exploring the codebase, so the implementing agent doesn't explore it again. Last in the body, under a `## 🤖 Agent Context` heading, which the platform skill turns into a collapsible. Where no platform skill covers the tracker, wrap it in GFM `<details>` at save time.
    68	
    69	Write lists of paths, symbols, and commands for an agent. [Style](#style) does not apply: line numbers, ranges, and bare enumeration are fine when they save a search.
    70	
    71	Emit only what exploration produced. Drop subsections you can't fill, and the whole section when exploration came up empty or you're filing in another project's tracker, whose maintainers know their own code. An issue in your own tracker about another project's bug keeps it.
    72	
    73	Open the block with one line, `Gathered at <commit> on <date>.` (`git rev-parse --short HEAD`), or `Gathered on <date>.` without a commit, and go straight to the first subsection. The implementer checks every pointer against their own checkout. That check already covers where a finding came from and what you couldn't confirm. State each finding as fact about the code. Pair every line number with its symbol, which survives drift.
    74	
    75	```markdown
    76	## 🤖 Agent Context
    77	
    78	Gathered at `a1b2c3d` on 1970-01-01.

    80	### Related Code
    81	
    82	- `acquire` at `src/pool.ts:88` blocks on an exhausted pool with no deadline
    83	- `release` at `src/pool.ts:140` early-returns on a closed connection, leaking the slot
    84	
    85	### Prior Art
    86	
    87	- `f0e9d8c` added the same deadline to the write pool. Mirror its test setup.

    93	|---------|---------|
    94	| Related Code | Files to change or read, with the symbol and why it matters |
    95	| Prior Art | Commits, PRs, or issues that solved a similar problem, and what to take |

   100	
   101	Human-facing body only. [Agent Context](#agent-context) has its own rules.
   102	
   103	State facts without hedging.
   104	
   105	Section headings are title-case noun phrases. Keep them free of sentences, slogans, and "X, not Y" antithesis. Write "Connection Lifecycle" rather than "Pin, don't invalidate".
   106	
   107	Use plain words over jargon and marketing. Drop terms like "spike" (as a verb), "seam", "disposition", "reality". Say what the thing does.
   108

    12	# Linear
    13	
    14	## Environment
    15	
    16	The connector and MCP paths need no CLI. Before a CLI-only operation (relations without the connector, bulk work), run `linear --version`, and stay on the connector when it fails. Check CLI subcommands and flags with `linear <cmd> --help` or the `linear-cli:linear-cli` skill.

    19

Pass `duplicateOf`, `parentId`, `project`, or `cycle` as `null` to clear one. `milestone` and `dueDate` have no `null` clear.

1	# Conventions
     2	
     3	House rules for writing to and querying Linear. Tool inputs below are JSON arguments for the connector and MCP tools named in [Tool Selection](../SKILL.md#tool-selection).
     4	
     5	## Issue References
     6	
     7	An issue reference renders as an inline chip only when Linear resolves it. The two write paths recognize opposite inputs:
     8	
     9	- **Connector `save_issue`**: reference an issue by its bare identifier, `ENG-123`. The connector resolves it to a clean `[ENG-123](url)` chip. A URL renders as a plain link, since the connector wraps it in `<>` and Linear stops recognizing it.
    10	- **CLI / GraphQL API**: reference an issue by its URL, either bare (`https://linear.app/workspace/issue/ENG-123`) or hyperlinked (`[the auth bug](https://linear.app/workspace/issue/ENG-123)`). A bare identifier stays literal text.
    11	- **Users, either path**: `@displayname` (for example `@bvdrucker`) chips a user mention on both paths, and is the most portable reference.
    12	
    13	Include the `url` field when querying issues you may reference in a CLI/API write.
    14	
    15	### Serialization and Round-Trip
    16	
    17	Storage is GFM markdown, the canonical interchange form. Raw GraphQL `description` and `linear issue view --json` return it byte-identical. The connector transforms it. On read it projects storage into node markup (`<issue>`, `<user>`, `<linear-embed>`), `>>>` collapsibles, and signed image URLs. On write it parses that markup back to GFM. When content moves between paths:
    18	
    19	- Store images by the unsigned `uploads.linear.app` URL the CLI/API return. Signed URLs (`?signature=…`) from a connector read expire within minutes.
    20	- Convert connector node markup to GFM before writing it through the CLI, or read the issue through the CLI/API to get GFM directly. The CLI stores node markup literally.
    21	- A `[ENG-123](url)` link read through the CLI loses its chip when written back through the connector, which `<>`-wraps it. To edit through the connector and keep chips, reference issues by bare identifier, or write through the CLI/API.
    22	
    23	## Collapsible Sections
    24	
    25	A collapsible renders collapsed, and its marker differs by write path the way [Issue References](#issue-references) do. The title sits on the opening marker. The closing marker is bare. Both need a blank line against the content. Markdown inside behaves normally, headings included.
    26	
    27	- **Connector `save_issue`**: `>>>`
    28	- **CLI / GraphQL API**: `+++` (the stored GFM form)
    29	
    30	```markdown
    31	+++ 🤖 Agent Context
    32	
    33	Gathered at `a1b2c3d` on 1970-01-01.
    34	
    35	+++
    36	```
    37	
    38	Issue refinement marks its collapsible as a `## 🤖 Agent Context` heading. Replace the heading with the opening marker for your path, keeping its text as the title, and close the block at the end of the body.
    39	
    40	## Issue Status
    41	
    42	Default a new issue's state from assignment: `Todo` when assigned to me, `Backlog` when unassigned. An explicit state from the user wins. The plugin's hooks apply this default on `save_issue`, `create_issue`, and single `linear issue create` invocations wherever its state options are set. Raw `linear api` mutations stay unhooked, so set `stateId` there, since an issue created with no state lands in Triage on a triage-enabled team.
    43	
    44	## CLI Idioms
    45	
    46	The CLI addresses the same fields with flags instead of connector JSON:
    47	
    48	- **Team** by key: `--team ENG` (the connector takes a team name or ID).
    49	- **Assignee**: `--assignee self` (the connector uses `"me"`).
    50	- **State** by name or type: `--state Todo` or `--state started`.
    51	- **Labels**: one `--label` per entry, repeated.
    52

    54	
    55	## Querying Issues
    56	
    57	Filter by `assignee: "me"` for the authenticated user's issues. Without an MCP list tool, fall back to GraphQL per [api.md](../api.md).
    58

    61	Pass label names directly, no IDs. Labels live at the workspace or team level, so when looking one up with `list_issue_labels`, check the workspace (`{}`) and then the team (`{ "team": "ENG" }`) before concluding it doesn't exist.

     3	The file carries issue metadata in YAML frontmatter and the body below the closing `---`. Keys vary by producer, so read the frontmatter for the keys it carries. Write the body to its own file so it passes by path and stays out of context.

    10	| body (below the closing `---`) | `description` |

    12	| `priority` (`urgent`, `high`, `medium`, `low`) | `priority` `1`..`4` |

    30	  "team": "ENG",
    31	  "title": "Fix authentication bug",
    32	  "description": "…",
    33	  "state": "Todo",
    34	  "blockedBy": ["ENG-100"],

1	# Load
     2	
     3	Paces Claude's heavy work to the machine it runs on. Unconfigured, it caps nothing and never reminds, so a VM can be saturated. On a machine shared with a person, configure it to remind the model to scale its work down as load climbs, with generous hard caps as a backstop.
     4	
     5	## Configuration
     6	
     7	Set these options under `pluginConfigs` in settings, keyed `load@<marketplace>`:
     8	
     9	- `browserSessions`: refuses to launch an `agent-browser` session while this many already run on the machine. `0` caps nothing. Each agent is held to one session regardless.
    10	- `caps`: `pool:limit:regex` entries. A Bash command matching an entry's regex is refused while `limit` processes in its pool already run, while it starts several at once (`&` in a loop, `xargs -P`), or under critical memory pressure. Entries sharing a pool share its limit. Running jobs are counted from `ps`, once per process tree, so wrappers and workers don't count twice.
    11	Thresholds are load average per core, named for what the mod does at each:
    12	
    13	- `remind`: after any tool call, appends a reminder to the result once load reaches it or memory is under pressure. The reminder names the load, memory pressure, Claude sessions, and capped jobs running, and asks the model to weigh its next heavy step: defer it, narrow it, or lower its worker and thread counts. `0` turns reminders off.
    14	- `warn`: a firmer reminder at this load, or under critical memory pressure, to start no heavy work the task doesn't need. Each agent hears each level once until the machine calms.
    15	- `refuse`: refuses capped commands while load is above it. `0` turns it off.
    16	
    17	[`user/settings.json`](../../user/settings.json) holds this repo's own values.
    18	
    19	## Contents
    20	
    21	- **Mod**: [`register.ts`](mod/register.ts) gates `Bash` calls, paces every tool call, and closes an agent's browser sessions when it ends.
    22	  - [`caps.ts`](mod/caps.ts) parses caps, samples the machine, and judges capped commands.
    23	  - [`pace.ts`](mod/pace.ts) grades the machine and writes the reminder.
    24	  - [`browser.ts`](mod/browser.ts) limits `agent-browser` to one session per agent and, when configured, a number of sessions machine-wide.
    25	  - [`command.ts`](mod/command.ts) splits a command line into the simple commands both read.
    26	- **Events**: launches, refusals, closes, reminders, and hook failures go to [`mod-events`](../mod-events/README.md) as `browser.*`, `cap.*`, `pace`, and `error`. `session.start` carries any caps that failed to parse.
    27	
    28	## Tests
    29	
    30	`bun scripts/mod-test.ts load` runs the mod's tests.

1	# Mac
     2	
     3	macOS-specific automation and system integration.
     4	
     5	## Contents
     6	
     7	### Skills
     8	
     9	- The **jxa** skill is a JXA language guide for writing JavaScript for Automation code.
    10	- The **jxa-run** skill is an app-scoped JXA runner with AST-based Application() validation.
    11	
    12	### Hooks
    13	
    14	- The **sandbox** hook reads the invoked script for the `claude:dangerouslyDisableSandbox` marker and disables the command sandbox when present. It matches both `Bash` and `Monitor` tool calls.
    15	- The `sandbox-ssh-proxy` hook runs at `SessionStart` and lets sandboxed git reach SSH remotes on macOS ([details](hooks/sandbox-ssh-proxy.md)).
    16	
    17	### Scripts
    18	
    19	- `scripts/jxa.ts` is an app-scoped JXA runner with AST-based `Application()` validation.
    20	- `scripts/open-url.ts` is a scheme-scoped URL opener with scheme validation.
    21	
    22	## Sandbox
    23	
    24	Go-based CLIs run fine sandboxed: `sandbox.network.allowMachLookup: ["com.apple.trustd.agent"]` in `user/settings.json` lets Go's `crypto/x509` reach the system `trustd` daemon for TLS verification (`gh`, `glab`, `terraform`, `kubectl`, `go`) profile-wide.
    25	
    26	Apple Events and Launch Services handoff is different. Scripts that shell out to `osascript` (JXA) or `open` (URL schemes) do not survive the sandbox even with `sandbox.allowAppleEvents`. They need a full skip.
    27	
    28	### Sandbox bypass marker
    29	
    30	The `sandbox` hook disables the command sandbox when the invoked script's first 64KB contains the literal string `claude:dangerouslyDisableSandbox`. It finds the script two ways: as the argument to `bun` or `node`, or as the command itself when a script is executed directly by path through its shebang and its extension is `.ts`, `.js`, `.mjs`, `.cjs`, or `.sh`.
    31	
    32	Two situations warrant the marker. One is handing off to Apple Events or Launch Services, which does not survive the sandbox. The other is writing a plugin's own data dir: the sandbox profile denies writes under `~/.claude/plugins`, and that deny shadows any `filesystem.allowWrite` entry beneath it. As a result, a plugin script cannot write `~/.claude/plugins/data/<plugin>-<marketplace>/` while sandboxed.
    33	
    34	Add the marker after the shebang:
    35	
    36	```ts
    37	#!/usr/bin/env bun
    38	// claude:dangerouslyDisableSandbox: hands off to osascript for JXA Apple Events
    39	```
    40	
    41	The marker goes on the top-level entrypoint script only. The hook inspects only the invoked script and never looks at imported modules. A helper like `things/scripts/ensure-running.ts` therefore doesn't carry a marker of its own. Its callers do.
    42	
    43	The marker is inert on Linux and inert when the `mac` plugin is not installed. It only activates when this hook runs on macOS.
    44	
    45	## Testing
    46	
    47	```bash
    48	bun test plugins/mac
    49	```

1	---
     2	name: mac:jxa
     3	disable-model-invocation: true
     4	description: Reference for writing JXA (JavaScript for Automation) scripts run through `osascript -l JavaScript`. Covers the JavaScriptCore ES5 constraints, `run(argv)`, and the `Application()` bridge.
     5	---
     6	
     7	# JXA
     8	
     9	JavaScript for Automation (JXA) automates macOS apps via the `Application()` bridge. It runs on JavaScriptCore (ES5).
    10	
    11	## Language Constraints
    12	
    13	- Use `var` (not `let`/`const`)
    14	- Use for-loops (JXA arrays lack `.map()`, `.filter()`, `.forEach()`)
    15	- Return a JSON string from `run()` (not an object)
    16	
    17	```javascript
    18	// WRONG: JXA arrays don't have .map()
    19	// var names = app.windows().map(function(w) { return w.name(); });
    20	
    21	// CORRECT: use a for-loop
    22	var windows = app.windows();
    23	var names = [];
    24	for (var i = 0; i < windows.length; i++) {
    25	  names.push(windows[i].name());
    26	}
    27	```
    28	
    29	## Script Files
    30	
    31	Script files define a `function run(argv)` entry point. `osascript` calls it and prints the return value. The function must be named `run`, not `_run`.
    32	
    33	```javascript
    34	#!/usr/bin/env osascript -l JavaScript
    35	function run(argv) {
    36	  var finder = Application("Finder");
    37	  var items = finder.desktop.items();
    38	  var names = [];
    39	  for (var i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {
    40	    names.push(items[i].name());
    41	  }
    42	  return JSON.stringify(names);
    43	}
    44	```
    45	
    46	## Tips
    47	
    48	- Use `properties()` for batch reads instead of individual getters
    49	- Use `.whose()` for filtering when the app supports it (pushes work to the app)
    50	- `Application.currentApplication()` accesses the current app context
    51	- Extract sdef for any app: `sdef /Applications/AppName.app`

1	# Meme
     2	
     3	Generate memes from images: classic Impact macros, labels, and TV-subtitle captions.
     4	
     5	## Skills
     6	
     7	- `image`: overlay meme text on an image (classic top/bottom, subtitle, caption bar, or multi-label spec)
     8	
     9	## Tests
    10	
    11	```sh
    12	bun test plugins/meme
    13	```

1	---
     2	name: image
     3	description: Generate a meme by overlaying text on an image. Use when asked to make a meme, caption an image, add meme text, or produce classic Impact macros, TV-subtitle stills, white-bar captions, or multi-label formats (Drake, distracted boyfriend, whiteboard).
     4	argument-hint: "[image-path] [meme text or idea]"
     5	allowed-tools:
     6	  - "Bash(bun ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/render.ts:*)"
     7	hooks:
     8	  PreToolUse:
     9	    - matcher: "Bash(bun ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/render.ts:*)"
    10	      hooks:
    11	        - type: command
    12	          command: "bun ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/skills/image/scripts/setup.ts"
    13	          once: true
    14	---
    15	
    16	# Meme Image
    17	
    18	Overlay meme text on an image with a deterministic renderer. You judge layout, placement, and legibility; the script guarantees the classic look (Impact stroke, subtitle yellow, caption bars).
    19	
    20	## Workflow
    21	
    22	1. Resolve the image. Use the user's path directly. If they name a meme format instead of a path, check the template library first (below). Otherwise WebSearch for the image and download with `curl -L -o tmp/<name>.jpg <url>`. Never pass a URL to the renderer.
    23	2. Read the image. Note the subjects, where faces and action are, contrast, and aspect ratio.
    24	3. Choose a mode:
    25	   - Top/bottom macro text: `--top` / `--bottom`
    26	   - TV-subtitle quote (yellow, bottom center): `--subtitle`
    27	   - White bar above or below the image: `--caption` (optionally `--caption-position top|bottom`, default top)
    28	   - Multi-label formats or custom placement: write a JSON spec file. Read [references/spec.md](references/spec.md) first.
    29	4. Pick the output filename. It is part of the joke: witty and meme-relevant, kebab or snake case, `.png`. Never `meme.png` or another generic name. If the user supplies a filename, use theirs.
    30	5. Render, then Read the output PNG. Check legibility, that text does not cover key subjects, line-break placement, and any fit warnings on stderr. Adjust and re-render until it reads well.
    31	6. Deliver: copy the file reference to the clipboard so a paste keeps the filename:
    32	
    33	   ```sh
    34	   osascript -e 'set the clipboard to POSIX file "<absolute output path>"'
    35	   ```
    36	
    37	   Report the path. If the clipboard copy is declined or fails, reveal the file instead: `open -R <path>`.
    38	
    39	## Template Library
    40	
    41	`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}/templates/` holds the user's meme templates, synced outside git. Never copy its images into the repo. Each image may have a sidecar spec of the same basename (`drake.jpg` + `drake.json`): a ready-made layout whose `text` values are `<slot descriptions>` and whose `description` says how the format works.
    42	
    43	- User names a format: `ls` the library and match by filename. With a sidecar, copy it to `tmp/`, replace each slot with the actual joke, and render with `--spec`. Panel counts matter: fill every slot the joke needs and drop boxes the format leaves empty.
    44	- No sidecar (new template): Read the image, trace regions, render, iterate. Once the layout looks right, save it back as a sidecar with `<slot description>` placeholders so the next use skips the tracing.
    45	
    46	## Rendering
    47	
    48	```sh
    49	bun ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/render.ts <image> [flags] -o tmp/<joke-name>.png
    50	```
    51	
    52	| Flag | Meaning |
    53	|------|---------|
    54	| `--top`, `--bottom` | Classic Impact macro text |
    55	| `--subtitle` | TV-subtitle text at the bottom |
    56	| `--caption` | White-bar caption (expands the canvas); `--caption-position top\|bottom` |
    57	| `--spec`, `-s` | JSON layout spec file (mutually exclusive with the text flags) |
    58	| `--out`, `-o` | Output PNG path (always required) |
    59	
    60	On success the script prints the absolute output path. Fit problems are warnings, not errors: the text still renders at the shrink floor. Treat every warning as a cue to shorten text or enlarge its region.
    61	
    62	## Gotchas
    63	
    64	- Web search returns template *pages*, not image files, and meme-site pages are often JS-rendered so the image URL is not in the static HTML. Imgflip: the direct image is `https://i.imgflip.com/<id36>.jpg` where `<id36>` is the numeric template ID from the page URL in base36 (`(55311130).toString(36)` → `wxica`). Always `file` the download to confirm it is an image before rendering.
    65	- Multi-panel formats: set `"linkFontSizes": true` in the spec so all panels share one font size instead of each fitting independently.
    66	- Images narrower than 400px are auto-upscaled 2x before drawing, so tiny templates still get readable text. Expect output dimensions to differ from the input.
    67	- Spec coordinates and font sizes are normalized (0-1 fractions of image dimensions). Judge placement from the Read image in fractions, not pixels: Read may downscale.

1	# Layout Spec
     2	
     3	JSON file passed via `--spec`. Use it for multi-label formats, custom placement, style overrides, or any text containing `!`. All coordinates and font sizes are normalized: positions and sizes are fractions of the image dimensions (font sizes are fractions of image height). Caption bars are added outside the image, so box coordinates always refer to the original image area.
     4	
     5	## Schema
     6	
     7	```json
     8	{
     9	  "boxes": [
    10	    {
    11	      "text": "required non-empty string",
    12	      "preset": "classic | label | subtitle (default classic)",
    13	      "anchor": "top | bottom | center (mutually exclusive with region)",
    14	      "region": { "x": 0.1, "y": 0.2, "w": 0.5, "h": 0.25 },
    15	      "align": "left | center | right (default center)",
    16	      "valign": "top | middle | bottom (default follows anchor; regions default middle)",
    17	      "style": {
    18	        "fill": "#rrggbb",
    19	        "stroke": "#rrggbb",
    20	        "fontSize": 0.08,
    21	        "font": "font family name",
    22	        "uppercase": true
    23	      }
    24	    }
    25	  ],
    26	  "captions": [
    27	    { "text": "required", "position": "top | bottom (default top)" }
    28	  ],
    29	  "linkFontSizes": false
    30	}
    31	```
    32	
    33	At least one box or caption is required. `style` fields are sparse overrides on the preset; `fontSize` sets the starting size, and text still shrinks if it does not fit. `linkFontSizes: true` re-fits every box at the smallest fitted size; use it for multi-panel formats (Drake, Gru) where mismatched panel text reads wrong.
    34	
    35	## Presets
    36	
    37	| Preset | Look | Defaults |
    38	|--------|------|----------|
    39	| `classic` | Impact, uppercase, white fill, thick black stroke | anchor top, max size 0.10 x H |
    40	| `label` | Helvetica bold, mixed case, black fill, thin white stroke | anchor center, max size 0.06 x H |
    41	| `subtitle` | Helvetica bold, mixed case, yellow `#ffe400`, black outline | anchor bottom, max size 0.045 x H |
    42	
    43	Yellow reads as closed captions. For quoted dialogue or stylized show text (song lyrics, character lines) that is not meant to look like captioning, override to white: `"style": { "fill": "#ffffff" }`.
    44	
    45	Anchors map to canned regions: top `{x: 0.05, y: 0.02, w: 0.9, h: 0.3}`, bottom `{x: 0.05, y: 0.68, w: 0.9, h: 0.3}`, center `{x: 0.05, y: 0.35, w: 0.9, h: 0.3}`.
    46	
    47	Fixed constants (not spec surface): line height 1.15, region padding 4% per side, shrink floor (classic 0.028 x H, absolute floor 12px). Text wraps automatically; explicit newlines collapse to spaces.
    48	
    49	## Worked Examples
    50	
    51	### Classic Macro (Flags, No Spec Needed)
    52	
    53	```sh
    54	render.ts photo.jpg --top "I'm telling you" --bottom "the tests pass on my machine" -o tmp/pepe-silvia-works-on-my-machine.png
    55	```
    56	
    57	### TV Subtitle (Flags)
    58	
    59	```sh
    60	render.ts still.jpeg --subtitle "♪ workin' hard for the money ♪" -o tmp/dolly-would-approve.png
    61	```
    62	
    63	Renders yellow bottom-center subtitle text. Unicode like ♪ works in both flags and specs.
    64	
    65	### Two-Panel Labels (Jim's Whiteboard, 421x475)
    66	
    67	One label box per whiteboard panel, regions traced from the Read image:
    68	
    69	```json
    70	{
    71	  "boxes": [
    72	    {
    73	      "text": "just one more refactor",
    74	      "preset": "label",
    75	      "region": { "x": 0.06, "y": 0.07, "w": 0.44, "h": 0.3 }
    76	    },
    77	    {
    78	      "text": "and the codebase will be clean",
    79	      "preset": "label",
    80	      "region": { "x": 0.08, "y": 0.57, "w": 0.46, "h": 0.26 }
    81	    }
    82	  ]
    83	}
    84	```
    85	
    86	### Drake Format (Two Right-Half Rows)
    87	
    88	```json
    89	{
    90	  "boxes": [
    91	    { "text": "rejected option", "preset": "label", "region": { "x": 0.52, "y": 0.05, "w": 0.45, "h": 0.4 } },
    92	    { "text": "preferred option", "preset": "label", "region": { "x": 0.52, "y": 0.55, "w": 0.45, "h": 0.4 } }
    93	  ]
    94	}
    95	```
    96	
    97	### Caption Bar Plus Overlay Text
    98	
    99	```json
   100	{
   101	  "captions": [{ "text": "staging and production", "position": "top" }],
   102	  "boxes": [{ "text": "They're the same picture.", "preset": "subtitle" }]
   103	}

1	# Flowchart Reference
     2	
     3	## Basic Syntax
     4	
     5	```mermaid
     6	flowchart TB
     7	    A[Rectangle] --> B(Rounded)
     8	    B --> C{Diamond}
     9	    C -->|Yes| D[[Subroutine]]
    10	    C -->|No| E[(Database)]
    11	```
    12	
    13	## Direction
    14	
    15	| Directive | Direction |
    16	|-----------|-----------|
    17	| `TB` / `TD` | Top to bottom |
    18	| `BT` | Bottom to top |
    19	| `LR` | Left to right |
    20	| `RL` | Right to left |
    21	
    22	Use `LR` for timelines and processes. Use `TB` for hierarchies and for diagrams too wide for `LR`.
    23	
    24	## Node Shapes
    25	
    26	| Syntax | Shape | Use For |
    27	|--------|-------|---------|
    28	| `[text]` | Rectangle | Actions, processes |
    29	| `(text)` | Rounded | Start/end points |
    30	| `{text}` | Diamond | Decisions |
    31	| `[[text]]` | Subroutine | Function calls |
    32	| `[(text)]` | Cylinder | Databases |
    33	| `((text))` | Circle | Events, triggers |
    34	| `>text]` | Flag | Async signals |
    35	| `{{text}}` | Hexagon | Preparation steps |
    36	
    37	## Edge Types
    38	
    39	| Syntax | Style |
    40	|--------|-------|
    41	| `-->` | Arrow |
    42	| `---` | Line (no arrow) |
    43	| `-.->`| Dotted arrow |
    44	| `==>` | Thick arrow |
    45	| `--text-->` | Arrow with label |
    46	| `-->\|text\|` | Arrow with label (alt) |
    47	
    48	## Subgraphs
    49	
    50	Subgraphs inherit the parent direction. Use them to group by component, team, or phase.
    51	
    52	```mermaid
    53	flowchart TB
    54	    subgraph auth[Authentication]
    55	        A[Login] --> B[Validate]
    56	        B --> C[Token]
    57	    end
    58	
    59	    subgraph api[API Layer]
    60	        D[Request] --> E[Handler]
    61	    end
    62	
    63	    C --> D
    64	```
    65	
    66	## Styling
    67	
    68	```mermaid
    69	flowchart LR
    70	    classDef default fill:#fff,stroke:#333
    71	    classDef highlight fill:#ff0,stroke:#f00,stroke-width:2px
    72	
    73	    A[Normal] --> B[Highlighted]:::highlight
    74	```

1	# Sequence Diagram Reference
     2	
     3	## Participants
     4	
     5	Declare participants in data-flow order to set their left-to-right position. Aliases shorten labels.
     6	
     7	```mermaid
     8	sequenceDiagram
     9	    participant C as Client
    10	    participant S as Server
    11	    participant D as Database
    12	
    13	    C->>S: Request
    14	    S->>D: Query
    15	    D-->>S: Result
    16	    S-->>C: Response
    17	```
    18	
    19	## Message Types
    20	
    21	| Syntax | Meaning |
    22	|--------|---------|
    23	| `->>` | Synchronous request |
    24	| `-->>` | Async/return response |
    25	| `--)` | Async message (no wait) |
    26	| `-x` | Lost message |
    27	| `--x` | Lost async message |
    28	
    29	## Activations
    30	
    31	`+` activates and `-` deactivates. Activations can nest.
    32	
    33	```mermaid
    34	sequenceDiagram
    35	    participant C as Client
    36	    participant S as Server
    37	
    38	    C->>+S: Request
    39	    S->>S: Process
    40	    S-->>-C: Response
    41	```
    42	
    43	## Control Flow
    44	
    45	```mermaid
    46	sequenceDiagram
    47	    participant C as Client
    48	    participant A as Service A
    49	    participant B as Service B
    50	
    51	    alt Valid
    52	        C->>A: Request
    53	    else Invalid
    54	        A-->>C: 400 Bad Request
    55	    end
    56	
    57	    opt Cache Hit
    58	        A-->>C: Cached Response
    59	    end
    60	
    61	    loop Retry 3 times
    62	        C->>A: Request
    63	    end
    64	
    65	    par
    66	        C->>A: Request A
    67	    and
    68	        C->>B: Request B
    69	    end
    70	```
    71	
    72	## Notes
    73	
    74	```mermaid
    75	sequenceDiagram
    76	    participant C as Client
    77	    participant S as Server
    78	
    79	    Note over C,S: TLS Handshake
    80	    C->>S: Request
    81	    Note right of S: Validate token

     4	
     5	```mermaid
     6	stateDiagram-v2

     8	    Idle --> Processing: start

    10	    Processing --> Failed: error

    55

1	# Mod Events
     2	
     3	Telemetry for mods. It adds `$.modEvents.emit`, which writes each mod's events to per-session JSONL. Each line is an OpenTelemetry log record, so a collector can tail the files, and the `observability:session` index ingests them as `mod_events`.
     4	
     5	- **Mod**: [`register.ts`](mod/register.ts) provides `emit` and records at session start whether the session is local or reached over mosh or ssh, with each attached client's reach for the multiplexer named by the `multiplexer` option (for example `herdr`). Empty, the default, classifies from `SSH_CONNECTION` alone.
     6	- **Types**: [`types/index.d.ts`](types/index.d.ts) declares `$.modEvents.emit`.
     7	
     8	## Emitting
     9	
    10	A mod lists `"dependencies": ["mod-events"]` in its `plugin.json`, adds `"../../mod-events/types"` to its `mod/tsconfig.json` `include`, and calls:
    11	
    12	```ts
    13	void $.modEvents.emit({ mod: "herdr", event: "herdr.call", ok: exitCode === 0, ms, detail: { command, exitCode, stderr } });
    14	```
    15	
    16	`emit` never rejects. Without this plugin enabled, the default `emit` drops events. Every mod emits `session.start` from its `session.start` hook, so a query can tell whether it was live.
    17	
    18	Records land in `<config>/mod-events/<session>/<mod>.<instance>.<n>.jsonl`, `<config>` being `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` or `~/.claude`. `<instance>` is the first event's timestamp, so a reload starts new files, and `<n>` rolls at 64 KB.
    19	
    20	## Format
    21	
    22	Each line is one OTel log record with the data model's field names, flat rather than wrapped in an OTLP `resourceLogs` envelope:
    23	
    24	```json
    25	{"timestamp":"2026-10-06T17:00:00.012Z","severity_text":"WARN","severity_number":13,"event_name":"herdr.herdr.call","attributes":{"command":"pane.report-agent","exitCode":1,"stderr":"…","duration_ms":12,"session.id":"<session-id>"},"resource":{"service.name":"claude-code","service.version":"2.1.291","claude_code.surface":"mosh"},"scope":{"name":"herdr"}}
    26	```
    27	
    28	- `timestamp` is ISO 8601 in UTC, like Claude Code's own `event.timestamp`.
    29	- `severity_text` is `INFO` (9), or `WARN` (13) when `ok` is false. A failing mod degrades the session without ending it, so nothing logs `ERROR`.
    30	- `event_name` is `<mod>.<event>`.
    31	- `attributes` holds `detail`, plus `duration_ms` from `ms` and `session.id`. Both keys match Claude Code's native OTel events, so a backend can join a mod's records to the session's own telemetry.
    32	- `resource` carries `service.name` (`claude-code`, as the native exporter uses) and `service.version`. Once the session's heartbeat has judged it, it also carries `claude_code.surface` (`local`, `mosh`, or `ssh`).
    33	- `scope.name` is the mod. The engine doesn't expose a calling plugin's version, so `scope` has no `version`.
    34	
    35	`$.fs` can only replace a file whole, so each event rewrites its chunk. The new text always extends the old, and a rolled chunk is never written again, so a tailer's fingerprint and offset stay valid. `$.fs.write` truncates and then writes in place rather than renaming a temp file over the chunk, and `$.fs` has no rename. A tailer polling inside that window reads an empty file. The collector's `filelog` receiver skips a file whose fingerprint is empty, then resumes at its offset once the bytes are back.
    36	
    37	## Collector
    38	
    39	An `otelcol-contrib` `filelog` receiver maps each line into a log record. `event_name` lands as the `event.name` attribute, as Claude Code's own events carry it:
    40	
    41	```yaml
    42	receivers:
    43	  filelog/mod_events:
    44	    include: ["${env:HOME}/.claude/mod-events/**/*.jsonl"]
    45	    start_at: beginning
    46	    operators:

1	# Known Blind Spots
     2	
     3	Full elaboration of the structural absences summarized in [`SKILL.md`](../SKILL.md) "Known Blind Spots". The `index-health` query detects drift the corpus can show. The six below are absences no query can surface, because nothing was ever indexed for them. `field-drift` covers the opposite case, a field the harness added that no query reads yet.
     4	
     5	## Thinking Text
     6	
     7	Claude Code persists thinking blocks as signature-only stubs. `content_items` rows with `type = 'thinking'` exist but carry no text. Reasoning is unsearchable from transcripts and must be intercepted at runtime (hooks) if needed. The volume is measurable even though the text is not: `$.message.usage.output_tokens_details.thinking_tokens` counts it, roughly 45% of output tokens since 2026-08-11.
     8	
     9	## Retention Floor
    10	
    11	`cleanupPeriodDays` deletes old session files and the index reaps their rows on the next refresh, so the corpus floor ratchets forward (see `corpus-window`). `~/.claude/history.jsonl` holds prompt-level history much further back but is not ingested.
    12	
    13	## Cloud and Mobile Sessions
    14	
    15	claude.ai web/mobile chats and cloud routines write no local JSONL. A `bridge-session` record marks only that a cloud bridge existed. The cloud side's content stays remote.
    16	
    17	## Offloaded Tool Results
    18	
    19	Large outputs are truncated to a `<persisted-output>` preview pointing at a sidecar file under `tool-results/`. The full output never enters the index, but it is recoverable rather than gone: `$.toolUseResult.persistedOutputPath` records the sidecar's path (838 rows, 351MB), and spot-checks found the files still on disk. Read one directly when an analysis turns on what a truncated result actually said.
    20	
    21	## Other Machines
    22	
    23	Only imported hosts exist. A machine never imported, or one gone stale (see `host-staleness`), is invisible rather than empty.
    24	
    25	## Fields With No Signal
    26	
    27	Present in the corpus, checked, and carrying nothing. `field-drift` will keep surfacing new fields, so record here anything that turns out to be constant. It saves the next pass the check.
    28	
    29	- `message.stop_details`: always null.
    30	- `message.usage.inference_geo`: `not_available` on 113,341 of 113,387 rows.
    31	- `service_tier` and `speed`: constant `standard`.
    32	- `toolUseResult.userModified`: false on all 39,363 rows.
    33	- `mode`: always `normal`.
    34	- `atis-latch.atis`: empty string.
    35	- `classifierMetaLines`: carries `repoVisibility` and nothing else.

     8	
     9	<!-- generated:queries -->
    10	- `activity`: Session interaction profile: one row per prompt source, plus interruptions, queued goals, scheduled fires, compactions, API retries, hook friction, and the distribution of permission modes.

    17	- `field-drift` [`new_days`, `cutoff_date`, `min_rows`]: Fields the harness started or stopped writing, on record kinds the corpus carried before and since.

    19	- `hook-blocks` [`hook`]: Hook overfiring, blocking events grouped by hook and normalized reason signature, including the PreToolUse denies `hook_events` never records.
    20	- `hooks` [`event`, `hook`]: Per-hook runs, friction rate, and latency corrected for host-wide slowdowns, one row per hook keyed by command (or `hook_name` when no command is recorded).
    21	- `index-health` [`min_active_days`, `new_days`, `stale_days`, `deny_window_days`, `refresh_days`, `refresh_slow_ms`, `projects_glob`]: The index auditing itself. Run it first in any analysis pass, since its alerts cap what the rest can claim.
    22	- `model-summary`: Assistant text item, message, session, and character counts per model.
    23	- `mods`: Whether each mod was live and healthy: the sessions it started in, the events it emitted, how many failed, and where the sessions were reached from.
    24	- `outcomes` [`ongoing_hours`]: Session terminal states (shipped, abandoned-with-edits, handed off, no artifact), the outcome side the activity queries never measure.
    25	- `permissions` [`denial_kind`, `limit`]: Denied tool calls, one row per denial, with the mechanism that stopped it and the signal that answered.
    26	- `plan-iterations` [`min_plans`]: One row per ExitPlanMode present, ordered within a session, measuring the append-only re-present signature.
    27	- `plan-sizes` [`threshold`]: Weekly trend of plan sizes, the steering metric for the plan plugin's ExitPlanMode size gate.
    28	- `prune-acceptance`: Per-class acceptance of prompting-audit proposals, per run and across the last two runs, for the retire-a-class rule.
    29	- `repeat-read-waste`: Repeat Reads split by cause, isolating the true context tax from pagination and fan-out.
    30	- `sandbox-bypass-effective-command` [`min_count`]: Bypassed commands by their real verb, ranked by frequency, with the split between bypasses that followed a failed sandboxed run (`justified`) and those that did not (`reflexive`): the `excludedCommands` candidates.
    31	- `sandbox-bypass-scaffold`: Weekly share of `dangerouslyDisableSandbox` calls whose commands already escape through `excludedCommands`, the `sandbox` plugin's retirement signal.
    32	- `sandbox-path-deny-recurrence`: `Operation not permitted` and adjacent Bash failures bucketed into concrete sandbox config gaps, with recurrence and date span.

    34	- `skill-activity`: Work attributed to each skill: assistant turns, sessions, and input, output, and cache tokens.
    35	- `skill-auto-vs-explicit` [`min_calls`]: Per skill, how invocations split between the model choosing it (`model_auto`), another skill chaining into it (`chained`), and the user typing its slash command (`explicit`).
    36	- `stats`: Tool usage breakdown with error rates and aggregate totals.

    38	- `text-export` [`role`, `model`, `min_chars`]: Dump cleaned prose from `text_content`, one row per text item, TSV-friendly.

    42	- `usage-timeline` [`session` (required), `bucket_minutes`]: One session's token burn per time bucket, with estimated cost and a context-size proxy.
    43	<!-- /generated:queries -->
    44	
    45	## On-Disk Queries
    46	
    47	These read files rather than the index, each through a self-defaulting glob that `SET VARIABLE` overrides and `~` expands to home. The two marked with an extension load it with `-cmd ".read resources/extensions.sql"` after `-init resources/limits.sql`. For a new markdown or YAML need, feed the glob to `read_markdown_sections` or `read_yaml_frontmatter` rather than reinventing regex parsing, and never materialize file bodies into a column.
    48	
    49	<!-- generated:on-disk-queries -->
    50	- `hook-config-vs-observed` [`hook`, `hook_config_glob`]: Hooks configured on disk but never observed firing in the index, left-joined so the `observed_fires = 0` rows surface.

    52	- `plan-sections` [`plans_glob`, `markdown` extension]: One row per markdown section across plan files on disk, joined to the session that produced each plan.
    53	- `skill-config-vs-observed` [`skill`, `plugin_skill_glob`, `user_skill_glob`, `project_skill_glob`, `yaml` extension]: Installed skills that never fire, the curation instrument: SKILL.md frontmatter on disk left-joined against observed `skill_calls` and typed slash commands, zero-fire first.
    54	<!-- /generated:on-disk-queries -->
    55	
    56	## Tables and Views
    57	
    58	Every table and view carries a `host` column (`local` for this machine, the label for imported ones). The `sessions` view adds `project_id` (`host || ':' || project_path`) for cross-host project identity.
    59	
    60	- `raw`: one row per JSONL line, **every record type** (chat, attachments, system events, permission modes, titles, queue ops, snapshots, and more), not just user/assistant. Pinned scalar columns (`host`, `session_id`, `type`, `project_path`, `git_branch`, `is_meta`, `is_sidechain`, `duration_ms`, `timestamp`, `input_tokens`, `output_tokens`, the four `cache_*_tokens`, `uuid`, `message_id`, `model`, `entrypoint`, `attribution_skill`/`plugin`/`agent`, `title` for title records, `content_text` for string prompts, `source_file`, `source_line`) plus a `data JSON` column that holds the full original line. Filter and group on a pinned column rather than its `data` path: it skips parsing the JSON. Pinned numerics use `TRY_CAST`, so a divergent value type yields NULL rather than failing the import.
    61	- `records`: universal union over `raw`, one row per line, with a normalized `kind` label (`type`, plus `subtype`/attachment kind when present) and the cross-cutting dimensions (`uuid`, `parent_uuid`, `permission_mode`, `version`, `slug`, `is_meta`, `is_sidechain`) every record may carry, plus full `data`. `SELECT kind, COUNT(*) FROM records GROUP BY kind` is the whole taxonomy. Reach into `data->>'$.path'` for anything not pinned. The `fields` view lists those paths.
    62	- `attachments`: one row per `attachment` record (the richest non-chat category: hooks, diagnostics, skill/tool listings, plan/auto mode, queued commands, command permissions). The two are near-duplicates and together are ~85-95% of `length(attachment::VARCHAR)`, so measuring raw attachment length overstates injection cost roughly 2x. Measure `attachment->'$.content'->>'$.content'` instead. No shipped query is currently affected: `catalog-reinjection-thrash-sessions` is the only query summing raw attachment length, and it is scoped to `skill_listing`/`deferred_tools_delta`.

Columns: `tool_use_id` (the Stop, shared with every hook attachment it produced), `command`, `duration_ms`, `prompt_text` (set when the entry is a queued prompt the harness re-injected at Stop rather than a configured hook, NULL for real hooks). The harness's own roster, so unlike `hook_events` it includes a hook that produced no output. Replayed summary records are deduped by uuid.

1	# Cross-Machine Import
     2	
     3	Procedures for listing, importing, re-syncing, and forgetting another machine's session history. Host semantics and the egress policy live in [`SKILL.md`](../SKILL.md) "Cross-Machine History". Read that first. Substitute every `<skill-dir>` below with the skill directory path from `SKILL.md`.
     4	
     5	## Listing Hosts
     6	
     7	```bash
     8	bun <skill-dir>/scripts/hosts.ts
     9	```
    10	
    11	Shows each host with its import time, egress policy, last index, rsync source, and a ready-to-run re-sync command.
    12	
    13	## Importing a Machine
    14	
    15	Copy the source machine's `~/.claude/projects/` into the import root, then register it. The `!` prefix runs the commands in the user's own shell, so SSH host-key trust and any 2FA stay in their hands.
    16	
    17	```bash
    18	mkdir -p ~/.claude/session-imports/<label>/projects
    19	rsync -avn --update <user@host>:.claude/projects/ ~/.claude/session-imports/<label>/projects/   # dry run
    20	rsync -av  --update <user@host>:.claude/projects/ ~/.claude/session-imports/<label>/projects/   # real copy
    21	bun <skill-dir>/scripts/import.ts --host <label> --source '<user@host>:.claude/projects/'
    22	```
    23	
    24	`import.ts` writes a manifest (dirs `0700`, manifest `0600`) recording the label, `--source`, and egress policy, then re-indexes. The whole `projects/` tree is copied even though only `*.jsonl` is indexed, because that tree is also the re-sync unit.
    25	
    26	## Re-syncing
    27	
    28	The source stored in the manifest doubles as the re-sync input, so refreshing is the same rsync line followed by `import.ts`:
    29	
    30	```bash
    31	rsync -av --update <source> ~/.claude/session-imports/<label>/projects/
    32	bun <skill-dir>/scripts/import.ts --host <label>
    33	```
    34	
    35	Re-running `import.ts` on a registered host leaves its manifest intact and re-indexes only the changed files. Change detection is a per-file catalog keyed on path plus (mtime, size), so `rsync -a` preserving old source mtimes is not a problem: a newly delivered file is a new path, and an updated file differs in mtime or size. `hosts.ts` prints the exact line per host.
    36	
    37	## Forgetting a Machine
    38	
    39	```bash
    40	bun <skill-dir>/scripts/forget.ts --host <label>
    41	```
    42	
    43	Deletes the host's rows from the index and removes its synced files. `local` cannot be forgotten.
    44	
    45	## Cloud Sessions
    46	
    47	Cloud sessions (claude.ai/code, project threads) run in containers the Mac never sees. The plugin's `SessionEnd` hook, and its `Stop` hook at most every 15 minutes, copy each cloud session's transcript and its subagents' transcripts to `CLAUDE_SESSION_UPLOAD_URL` (`s3://bucket/prefix`), one object per file at `<prefix>/<remote-session-id>/...`, overwritten as it grows. A VM reclaimed without `SessionEnd` loses at most the last interval, unless the session is reopened, since its first upload in the new container carries the restored history. The hooks do nothing unless that variable is set in the cloud environment and `CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE` is `true`. Register the prefix as a host once, then pull:
    48	
    49	```bash
    50	mkdir -p ~/.claude/session-imports/cloud/projects
    51	bun <skill-dir>/scripts/import.ts --host cloud --source 's3://<bucket>/<prefix>/' --egress
    52	bun <skill-dir>/scripts/pull.ts --host cloud
    53	```
    54	
    55	`--egress` fits because these rows came from the cloud in the first place. The bucket keeps every session. `pull.ts` keeps the local copy to the sessions uploaded within `--days` (default 90, matching `cleanupPeriodDays`), fetching any whose objects grew and deleting the rest, so the next refresh imports the new ones and reaps the rows of the old, the way `cleanupPeriodDays` works for `local`. It shells out to the `aws` CLI with whatever credentials the environment provides.

1	# History-Discovery Recipe
     2	
     3	Fan out read-only analysts over the session index to mine config-change candidates, ground every candidate against the live config, then emit a ranked digest. `improve-claude-code`'s Discover mode drives this recipe. The digest is done when every candidate carries its SQL, `grounded`, and `confidence`.
     4	
     5	## Fan-Out
     6	
     7	1. Run `scripts/refresh.ts --refresh` once and let it finish before any agent starts. Agents only read, and their prompts name the DB path from `SKILL.md`.
     8	2. Audit the instrument before trusting it: `duckdb -readonly -json -init resources/limits.sql <db-path> < resources/queries/index-health.sql`. Every alert constrains the run: a `stream-silent` kind means the dimensions reading it (e.g. diagnostics) return stale or empty results with no error; a `stream-migrated` kind is still live under the successor field its detail names, so read that field instead of treating the kind's zero as an absence; a stale host means cross-host numbers read that machine as idle; `null-timestamp-kinds` lists rows every date-scoped query excludes. Pass the alerts to the agents, and cite them in the digest wherever they cap a finding's confidence.
     9	3. `index-health`'s `field-new` and `field-dead` count the fields the harness started or stopped writing on record kinds the index already carried, and `field-drift` lists them. A hit means a query somewhere is inferring what the harness now states, so read it as a backlog item rather than as a constraint on the current run.
    10	4. Fan out one `analyst` agent per dimension below, which reads at its own cheaper model default. Each runs its named queries (`duckdb -readonly -json -init resources/limits.sql <db-path> < resources/queries/<name>.sql`, scoped with `SET VARIABLE`) plus any inline rollups against the one shared file.
    11	5. Each agent returns at most six candidate findings in about 2,500 characters total, each with the SQL that produced it: a named query plus its `SET VARIABLE` params, or a short inline statement. Results that finish together share one capped delivery, so an oversized return arrives truncated. Recover one from the agent's transcript, `~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session-id>/subagents/agent-<id>.jsonl`, whose longest assistant text block is the full report.
    12	6. One or more grounding agents re-check every candidate (see [Grounding](#grounding)). They need `WebFetch`, which `analyst` lacks, so spawn them generic with a cheap `model`.
    13	
    14	## Dimension Cheat Sheet
    15	
    16	Each dimension maps to the named queries that answer it ([`catalog.md`](catalog.md)) and the survey surfaces to start from. Write simple `GROUP BY ... COUNT/SUM` rollups inline.
    17	
    18	This table and the Tier-2 list below are generated from the `-- ---` headers on `resources/queries/*.sql`. Edit the header, then regenerate with `UPDATE_QUERY_CATALOG=1 bun test plugins/observability/skills/session`.
    19	
    20	<!-- generated:dimensions -->
    21	| Dimension | Named queries | Survey surfaces |
    22	|-----------|---------------|-----------------|
    23	| Hook latency | `hook-self-timing` | `hooks` |
    24	| Hook blocks | `hook-block-then-retry-success` | `hook-blocks`, `hooks` |
    25	| Hook coverage | `hook-config-vs-observed` | `hooks` |
    26	| Permissions and sandbox | `already-allowed-still-prompting`, `sandbox-bypass-effective-command`, `sandbox-bypass-scaffold`, `sandbox-path-deny-recurrence` | `permissions`, `sandbox_bypasses` |
    27	| Tool failures | `cli-health`, `tool-failure-rates` | `tool-failure-rates` |
    28	| Context tax | `catalog-reinjection-thrash-sessions` | `activity`, `hooks` (additionalContext) |
    29	| Tokens | `delegation`, `repeat-read-waste`, `top-sessions` | `stats`, `model-summary`, `skill-activity` |
    30	| Turns and compaction | `stop-hook-noop-detector` | `activity` (compactions, API errors) |
    31	| Skill economy | `skill-auto-vs-explicit` | `skill_calls`, `skill-activity` |
    32	| Planning | `plan-iterations` | `plan_sessions`, `plan_calls` |
    33	| Outcomes | `outcomes` | `pr_links`, `plan_calls`, `file_operations` |
    34	<!-- /generated:dimensions -->
    35	
    36	Use `records` and `fields` whenever a dimension needs a path that isn't pinned: `SELECT kind, COUNT(*) FROM records GROUP BY kind` is the full taxonomy, and `fields` lists every path two levels down per record type.
    37	
    38	## Grounding
    39	
    40	Re-check every candidate against the live config repo, the git toplevel of `dirname "$(readlink ~/.claude/settings.json)"`. Drop the candidate if the config already addresses it; downgrade it if the evidence is thin or host-skewed. Carry two fields per candidate:
    41	
    42	- `grounded` (boolean): the finding survived the re-check against live config.
    43	- `confidence` (high/medium/low): how strong the grounded evidence is.
    44	
    45	- Hooks run in parallel. Report wait time as the slowest matching hook plus a fixed per-process overhead. A sum over `hook_events.duration_ms` is aggregate process work.
    46	- `hook_events` never records a PreToolUse deny, so the `blocks` and `friction_pct` columns in `hooks` understate a denying hook, often to zero. Read `hook-blocks` (which unions the recovered `hook_denies` rows) before calling a hook low-friction, and check `index-health`'s `hook-deny-invisible` for how much of the deny channel is dark in the window you are mining.
    47	- A subagent's transcript lines carry the PARENT session's id, so `session_id` alone cannot separate a parent's own tool calls from its fan-out's. `hook_denies` is where this bites hardest, because a recovered deny comes from a tool_result and subagents produce those in volume: a discovery run's own mining subagents each hitting a hook once reads as one enormous burst by the orchestrator. Key any per-session claim over `tool_calls`, `tool_errors`, or `hook_denies` on `agent_id` as well (`hook-blocks` does), and read `subagent_blocks` before calling a hook a storm.
    48	- An aggregate spanning a fix reports a closed bug as current. Before citing a block or deny count, compare the signature's `first_seen`/`last_seen` against the git history of the hook that produced it: a count that stops at the commit that fixed the hook is evidence the fix worked, not evidence of friction. Split the window at that commit and re-run rather than reporting the total.
    49	- Explicitness of a skill invocation does not live on the Skill call. Typing `/name` expands into a user message carrying a `<command-name>` marker, and args on a Skill call are ordinary model routing. `skill-auto-vs-explicit` splits those two populations, and a `disable-model-invocation` finding rests on its `explicit` column.
    50	- A hook's `p95_ms` is not attributable until `excess_p95_ms` confirms it. Host-wide slowdowns inflate every hook in the same hour by the same factor, `bash` and `bun` alike, so the highest-volume hooks sample those windows most and look slow. Check `ambient_p50_ms` before filing a latency finding. Where a hook self-times its own work (the `writing` PreToolUse dispatcher writes `duration_ms` to `~/.claude/writing-hooks/log.jsonl`), that in-process figure beats the harness duration, which includes process spawn and interpreter start.
    51	- Split attachment and injection counts by `isSidechain` before making any per-session claim about them. Per-subagent context (the skill catalog, the deferred-tools delta) is injected once per subagent, so a session total scales with fan-out and any co-scaling variable will look causal.
    52	- Catalog and deferred-tools reinjection volume is not itself a finding. The harness controls when it reinjects, and no config change here reduces it. Injections fire on resume as well as at a `system:compact_boundary`, which is why a window's total runs large even when actual compaction is rare. Use the volume as an input to valuing catalog and skill-description tokens, since those pay repeatedly per session rather than once, and stop there rather than filing it as a candidate.
    53	- Split friction into the part a setting can change and the part it cannot. `ExitPlanMode` and `AskUserQuestion` rejections are not allowlistable; the named `permissions` query already excludes them, so only custom SQL over `permission_requests`/`tool_errors` needs that filter. A compound command escapes the sandbox only when every top-level command matches `excludedCommands`, so `cd <dir> && <exempt verb>` and an exempt verb piped into another command run sandboxed, and a bypass on either can have a real sandbox cause. Counting raw rejections without that split inflates the actionable set.
    54	- Sort a `tool-failure-rates` signature by what would fix it. `StructuredOutput` and `ReportFindings` failures are schema-validation retries, fixed in the schema or the prompt that fills it, and the model usually passes on its next call. A harness tool rejecting its input (`EnterWorktree` refusing a path, `TaskStop` on a finished task) points at the skill or instruction that issued the call.
    55	- A query studying the plan gate specifically cannot trust `denial_kind` on `ExitPlanMode`. The harness sets `$.toolDenialKind` to `permission-rule` for any PreToolUse-shaped deny, which covers plannotator's structured feedback block and plain freeform human rejections alongside an actual `plugins/plan/hooks/gate.ts` deny. Identify a genuine gate deny by matching `error_content` against the four rules the gate enforces, using substrings that survive its rewordings: `unchanged` or `byte-identical` for unchanged text, `nearly every` or `nearly all` for append-only, `is larger than any before it` for sustained growth, and `k characters` for size, which covers both the first-pass and the re-armed wording. The gate's phrasing has been rewritten repeatedly, so matching its current templates literally misses every earlier wording.
    56	- A `disable-model-invocation: true` proposal is breaking if any other skill invokes the target via the `Skill` tool. The current binary blocks `Skill()` on a disabled skill even when the caller grants `Skill(<name>)` in its `allowed-tools`. Before grounding such a finding, grep `plugins` and `user` for `Skill(<name>)` and for the skill's name in other skills' bodies; a single cross-skill consumer fails it. Confirming only that the frontmatter key is absent is not enough.
    57	
    58	Verify any claim about harness behavior against the primary Claude Code docs, not a paraphrase, before grounding a finding on it.
    59	
    60	## Host Safety
    61	
    62	The index spans every machine. `local` is this machine; imported hosts carry their own label and may be marked `block_egress` (see `SKILL.md` "Cross-Machine History").
    63	
    64	- Aggregate across hosts, but label the host on every row. The queries here already select `host`.
    65	- Default to `host = 'local'` for any config-change candidate. The config you are changing is this machine's. Use other hosts only as corroborating aggregate ("this also shows up on `work`"), never as the sole evidence for a local change.
    66	- Never paste raw `content`, `command`, `stdout`, or `text` from an egress-blocked host verbatim into a digest, a todo, a PR, or anything else that leaves the machine. Quote `local` rows when you need a literal; cite imported hosts as counts only.

1	---
     2	name: opentelemetry
     3	description: >-
     4	  OpenTelemetry instrumentation conventions. Use when instrumenting code with
     5	  spans, setting up tracing, or writing trace tests.
     6	user-invocable: true
     7	disable-model-invocation: true
     8	---
     9	
    10	# OpenTelemetry
    11	
    12	## Span Naming
    13	
    14	Use short, low-cardinality names from semantic conventions:
    15	
    16	- HTTP: `GET /users/{id}` (method + route template, never full URL path)
    17	- DB: `SELECT users` (operation + table)
    18	- RPC: `grpc.health.v1.Health/Check`
    19	- Messaging: `orders process` (destination + operation)
    20	
    21	## Attributes
    22	
    23	Use [semantic convention](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/) attribute names — never invent your own:
    24	
    25	- HTTP: `http.request.method`, `url.full`, `http.response.status_code`, `server.address`
    26	- DB: `db.system`, `db.statement`, `db.namespace`
    27	- General: `error.type`, `service.name`
    28	
    29	Import from the versioned semconv package (e.g., `go.opentelemetry.io/otel/semconv/v1.x`).
    30	
    31	## Status
    32	
    33	Only set status on errors: `span.SetStatus(codes.Error, err.Error())`. Never set `Ok` — unset is the success state. Call `RecordError` alongside `SetStatus`; it only adds a span event, doesn't change status.
    34	
    35	For HTTP: 4xx is `Error` on client spans, `Unset` on server spans. 5xx is always `Error`.
    36	
    37	## Testing
    38	
    39	Use in-memory exporters with `SimpleSpanProcessor` (not batch — batch introduces timing). Assert on exported spans' names, attributes, and status. No mocking needed.
    40	
    41	## Boundaries
    42	
    43	Instrument network calls, I/O, and queue operations — not every function. Use span events (`AddEvent`) instead of separate log statements for events within a traced operation.

1	# performance
     2	
     3	Profile, benchmark, and hill-climb software performance with noise-aware measurement.
     4	
     5	## Skills
     6	
     7	- `performance:profile`: rank where a program's time goes with `samply`, runtime profilers, or browser traces, and what holds its peak memory with `malloc_history` or `heaptrack`
     8	- `performance:benchmark`: compare versions with interleaved `hyperfine` rounds, A/A noise floors, and permutation tests
     9	- `performance:hill-climb`: improve a metric one measured change at a time, with the user reviewing the framing and early iterations
    10	
    11	## Tests
    12	
    13	```bash
    14	bun test plugins/performance
    15	```

1	---
     2	name: performance:benchmark
     3	description: >-
     4	  Use when timing a program or command, asking whether a change or version
     5	  made it faster, or building a benchmark harness. To hill-climb or
     6	  repeatedly optimize toward a target, use performance:hill-climb.
     7	argument-hint: "[<command>]"
     8	---
     9	
    10	# Benchmark
    11	
    12	Goal: a comparison the user can trust. Every arm runs the same scenario from the same starting state, the arms are interleaved so machine drift hits them equally, the noise floor is measured before any difference is read, and a difference counts only when it clears that floor.
    13	
    14	## Tools
    15	
    16	- `hyperfine` 2.0 or later: !`hyperfine --version 2>/dev/null || echo "not found. Required unless the project's own tooling covers its job."`
    17	- `bun` (runs `compare.ts`): !`bun --version 2>/dev/null || echo "not found. Required for compare.ts."`
    18	
    19	## Existing Tooling
    20	
    21	Look for the project's own benchmarks before building one: package scripts, a `bench/` directory, benchmark tests, CI jobs that time something. Check each against the requirements the setup below is built to meet:
    22	
    23	- **Scenario.** It runs the scenario the user cares about, from the same starting state every run.
    24	- **Isolation.** Network, remote state, and caches are stubbed, held fixed, or reset per run.
    25	- **Interleaving.** Arms alternate within one run or one process, so drift hits every arm.
    26	- **Samples.** It keeps every run's measurement, enough of them to show an A/A noise floor, not only a mean.
    27	- **Significance.** It reports a significance test, or its samples can feed `compare.ts report`.
    28	
    29	Use the existing tooling when it meets every requirement. When it misses some, compose around it and keep its scenario: run its command as a `compare.ts` arm for interleaving and significance, or add a `--prepare` reset. Tell the user which requirement it missed and what you added.
    30	
    31	## Scenario
    32	
    33	Pin the scenario before timing it. A run that changes its own input measures a different scenario each time.
    34	
    35	- Reset state per run with `--prepare` (restore a fixture, clear or warm a cache), and one-time setup with `--setup`. Match the cache state to the scenario the user cares about. A cold-start metric needs a cold cache on every run.
    36	- Stub or hold fixed everything outside the program: network, remote state, other processes' files. When the program syncs with a remote, point it at a local copy that stays unchanged.
    37	- Pass `-N` when the command is a single executable with arguments, which removes the shell's startup from every sample.
    38	- Before a baseline, put the machine on AC power with power saving off, and quiet it as far as it goes. When it cannot go idle, interleaving keeps the comparison fair. `compare.ts` records the load average around each round and flags rounds above twice the core count.
    39	- When the program is a test suite, raise the runner's timeout in every arm's command (`bun test --timeout`, `pytest --timeout`), so a load spike slows a run instead of failing it. Read the first timeout before raising it, since it can be a real cost worth a candidate.
    40	- For a shell script or shell startup (`.zshrc`, `.bashrc`), read [references/shell.md](references/shell.md).
    41	
    42	## Arms
    43	
    44	Interleaving runs every arm in the same round, so each one exists on disk at once:
    45	
    46	- **Copies.** A `git worktree add <dir> <ref>` per version, or a separate build output per arm. Put each worktree under the repo's gitignored `tmp/arms/`, and exclude that directory from any test runner, linter, or watcher that walks the tree. A comparison ends once `report` has printed, so remove its arms then with `git worktree remove --force tmp/arms/<arm>`.
    47	- **State.** When the program writes outside its tree (`~/.cache`, a config directory), point each arm at its own copy. Shared state lets a candidate that changes a cache format make both arms miss on every run.
    48	- **Paths.** Check that each arm runs only its own copy. A test runner reads a bare path argument as a filter that can match another arm's tree, so pass paths with a leading `./`.
    49	- **Passing run.** Before a long comparison, run each arm once with its output visible and confirm it passes.
    50	
    51	Compare with the bundled script, which runs short `hyperfine` rounds in rotating order and pools them:
    52	
    53	```bash
    54	bun ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/compare.ts run tmp/bench/<comparison> \
    55	  --hypothesis '<change and predicted effect>' --arm 'base=<command>' --arm 'candidate=<command>' --rounds 6 --runs 3 -- -N --prepare '<reset>'
    56	bun ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/compare.ts report tmp/bench/<comparison> --markdown
    57	```
    58	
    59	The first `--arm` is the base. Arguments after `--` go to every `hyperfine` call. Give each comparison its own directory, since `run` refuses one that already holds exports. `run` writes the hypothesis and per-round load to `meta.json` there, and `report` prints both above the table. When a round is flagged, it adds a second table pooled without the flagged rounds. `report` also reads `--export-json` files from a plain `hyperfine` run, and pools every file and directory it is given per arm name.
    60	
    61	## Noise Floor
    62	
    63	Before comparing versions, run the unchanged program as two arms (an A/A comparison) and repeat until the pair ties. When it stars, the harness is noisier than the effect:
    64	
    65	- Raise `--runs` or `--rounds`.
    66	- Quiet the machine.
    67	- Find the state that leaks between runs.
    68	
    69	The A/A spread (`±MAD`) is the smallest change the harness can resolve.
    70	
    71	When the Mac's A/A will not tie, machine load would delay a comparison by more than about 15 minutes, or the fast signal needs `perf` or hardware counters, read [../profile/references/linux-vm.md](../profile/references/linux-vm.md).
    72	
    73	## Reading the Report
    74	
    75	- `*` marks a change with permutation p below `--alpha` (0.1) and a size of at least `--min-effect` (3%). An unstarred change is a tie, however large it looks.
    76	- `†` marks fewer than 4 runs on a side, too few to star. With 3 a side, the permutation test cannot reach p < 0.1 however far apart the arms are, so plan `--rounds` and `--runs` for at least 4 per arm, even when each run is expensive.
    77	- A nonzero `failed` count means some runs exited nonzero and left the pool. `compare.ts run` stops after the round where a run fails. Run that arm once with its output visible and fix the cause before starting a new comparison.
    78	- About one comparison in ten stars by chance at the default alpha. Re-run a star on a metric nobody predicted would move before treating it as a result.
    79	
    80	## Memory
    81	
    82	`compare.ts` records each run's peak resident set size (max RSS) from `hyperfine`, beside wall time. When the goal is memory, peak RSS is the metric: `compare.ts report <dir> --metric memory` runs the same significance test and star rule on it.
    83	
    84	- Judge a memory candidate on peak RSS with significance, never on total bytes allocated. Allocation volume tracks allocator time, and a change can cut it while the peak stays put.
    85	- Each run's peak RSS is that of the largest single process, read through `getrusage` of the child. Pass `-N` so it is the program's own, not a shell's. A program that spreads its peak over child processes needs each child measured.
    86	- Arms that each repeat one exact value differ deterministically, and the report gives that difference p = 0.
    87	- Outside `compare.ts`, read peak RSS with `/usr/bin/time -l` on macOS (bytes) or `/usr/bin/time -v` on Linux (KB), or from `resourceUsage().maxRSS` of a `Bun.spawn` child, which works inside the sandbox.
    88	- macOS reports `peak memory footprint` beside max RSS. Footprint excludes mapped binary text and shared pages, so the two differ. Name the one the climb records and compare like with like.
    89	
    90	To find what holds the peak, profile it with `performance:profile`.
    91	
    92	## Fast Signals
    93	
    94	Wall time is the metric users feel, and the noisiest. A fast signal screens candidates cheaply and confirms with lower noise. Before trusting one, check on the baseline that it moves with wall time.
    95	
    96	- **CPU and counters.** `perf stat` on Linux and `/usr/bin/time -l` on macOS report instructions retired, cycles, and peak memory. Instructions retired vary far less than wall time. `time -l` counts the top process only, not its children, and reads a sysctl the Bash sandbox denies.
    97	- **Microbenchmarks.** When a candidate changes one hot function, benchmark that function in-process, per the language's reference: [JavaScript](references/javascript.md) (Bun, Node), [Go](references/go.md) (`testing`, `benchstat`), [Rust](references/rust.md) (`criterion`, `divan`, instruction counts), [Python](references/python.md) (`pytest-benchmark`).
    98	- **Work counts.** Deterministic counts (renders, queries, syscalls, bytes written) have no noise. Count them wherever the program exposes them.
    99	
   100	## Gotchas
   101	
   102	- `hyperfine` runs each command's runs back to back. Two separate `hyperfine` invocations minutes apart carry drift between them, so compare arms inside one interleaved run.
   103	- A benchmark built from a debug or profiling build measures that build. Check the build flags against what users run.
   104	- Few rounds produce differences that flip sign on a re-run. When a result surprises, re-run it at more rounds before acting on it.
   105	- Synthetic inputs whose shape differs from real ones (size, cardinality, nesting) can invert a conclusion. Confirm on real inputs.

     2	
     3	## Whole Programs
     4	
     5	Build the binary once per arm with `go build -o tmp/bench/<arm>/<bin>` and benchmark the binaries. `go run` compiles on every start and measures the compiler.
