     7	## Microbenchmarks
     8	
     9	Write `testing` benchmarks with `b.Loop()` (Go 1.24+), which keeps the compiler from removing the measured call:
    10	
    11	```go
    12	func BenchmarkParse(b *testing.B) {
    13		input := loadRealInput(b)
    14		for b.Loop() {
    15			Parse(input)
    16		}
    17	}
    18	```
    19	
    20	On older Go, loop to `b.N`, assign the result to a package-level variable, and build the input before `b.ResetTimer()`.
    21	
    22	Compare arms with `benchstat`, which reports a p-value per benchmark and prints `~` when the difference is not significant:
    23	
    24	```bash
    25	go test -run '^$' -bench <Name> -benchmem -count 10 ./<pkg> > tmp/bench/base.txt
    26	benchstat tmp/bench/base.txt tmp/bench/candidate.txt
    27	```
    28	
    29	- Two `go test` runs minutes apart carry drift between them. Interleave instead: compile each arm's test binary once with `go test -c -o tmp/bench/<arm>.test`, then alternate `-test.bench <Name> -test.count 1` between the binaries in a loop, appending to each arm's file.

1	# JavaScript and TypeScript
     2	
     3	## Whole Programs
     4	
     5	Benchmark a CLI or script through `hyperfine` like any other command. Decide what startup the scenario includes:
     6	
     7	- `bun script.ts` transpiles on every start. A CLI users run as a bundled or compiled binary (`bun build --compile`, `bun build --target=bun`) is measured in that form.
     8	- `node --import tsx script.ts` and similar loaders add their own startup. Measure the form users run.
     9	- Separate startup from work when the climb targets one of them: time `bun -e ''` or an import-only entry alongside the full run.
    10	
    11	## Microbenchmarks
    12	
    13	Use [`mitata`](https://github.com/evanwashere/mitata) to benchmark a function in-process. It runs on Bun and Node, handles warmup and JIT tiering, and reports percentiles.
    14	
    15	```ts
    16	import { bench, do_not_optimize, run } from "mitata";
    17	
    18	bench("base", () => do_not_optimize(baseImpl(input)));
    19	bench("candidate", () => do_not_optimize(candidateImpl(input)));
    20	await run();
    21	```
    22	
    23	- Pass every result through `do_not_optimize`. The JIT removes a call whose result is unused, and the benchmark then times an empty loop.
    24	- Build `input` outside the benchmark body, from real data where possible. A tiny or uniform input hits paths real inputs never take.
    25	- Put both implementations in one file so they share a process and interleave. Comparing two separate runs reintroduces drift.
    26	- Treat a microbenchmark win as a screen. Confirm it on the whole program, since a faster function on a cold path leaves the user-facing metric unchanged.

1	# Python
     2	
     3	## Whole Programs
     4	
     5	Benchmark a Python CLI through `hyperfine` like any other command. Interpreter startup and imports often dominate short commands. Measure them alone with `python -X importtime -c 'import <module>'`, which prints a per-module import time tree to stderr.
     6	
     7	## pytest-benchmark
     8	
     9	Use `benchmark.pedantic()` with explicit `rounds`, `iterations`, and `warmup_rounds` for a comparison. The default auto-calibration picks a different round count per variant.
    10	
    11	- Parametrize both variants into one session, so they share a process and machine state. A `--benchmark-compare` against a result saved minutes earlier carries the drift between the two sessions.
    12	- Run at least 25 rounds before reading a difference. At 5 rounds, differences between high-variance cases flip sign on a re-run.
    13	- `pedantic` calls the same target with the same arguments every round. Any object passed in that holds state (a sampler, a connection, a stop flag) must reset itself on each call, or every round after the first measures a stale object.
    14	- Pass `-p no:randomly` and `--timeout=0` when the suite uses `pytest-randomly` or `pytest-timeout`, so ordering and timeouts stay fixed across variants.
    15	- Export with `--benchmark-json` and keep the files beside the notes.
    16	
    17	## Real Inputs
    18	
    19	Benchmark against real data before trusting a conclusion. Synthetic data with the wrong size, cardinality, or distribution has inverted conclusions that real inputs then reversed.

1	# Rust
     2	
     3	## Whole Programs
     4	
     5	Benchmark `target/release/<bin>`, built once per arm into its own target directory (`CARGO_TARGET_DIR=tmp/bench/<arm>`). `cargo run` checks the build on every start. Build with the release settings users get.
     6	
     7	## Microbenchmarks
     8	
     9	Use the harness the project already has. For a new one, use [`criterion`](https://github.com/bheisler/criterion.rs): a benchmark group runs both arms in one process and reports whether their difference exceeds noise. When the metric is allocations, add [`divan`](https://github.com/nvzqz/divan) for its `AllocProfiler`, whose counts are deterministic. Pass inputs and results through `std::hint::black_box`, or the optimizer removes the measured work.
    10	
    11	```rust
    12	fn bench(c: &mut Criterion) {
    13	    let input = load_real_input();
    14	    let mut group = c.benchmark_group("parse");
    15	    group.bench_function("base", |b| b.iter(|| parse_base(black_box(&input))));
    16	    group.bench_function("candidate", |b| b.iter(|| parse_candidate(black_box(&input))));
    17	    group.finish();
    18	}
    19	```
    20	
    21	- Put both implementations in one benchmark group so they share a process and machine state. `criterion`'s `--save-baseline` and `--baseline` compare against a run from earlier, which carries the drift between the two runs.
    22	- `criterion` prints "No change in performance detected" when the difference is within noise. Treat that as a tie.
    23	
    24	## Instruction Counts
    25	
    26	On Linux, [`gungraun`](https://github.com/gungraun/gungraun) (formerly `iai-callgrind`) runs benchmarks under Valgrind and reports instructions and cache accesses. The counts barely vary between runs, so they make a strong fast signal. Check on the baseline that they track wall time.

1	# Shell
     2

     4	
     5	Benchmark a shell script through `hyperfine` like any other command. Leave out `-N` when the command needs a shell to parse it. `hyperfine` then subtracts its own shell's startup from each sample.
     6	
     7	## Startup
     8	
     9	Measure interactive startup with `hyperfine 'zsh -i -c exit'` (or `bash -i -c exit`).
    10	
    11	- Compare config trees by giving each arm its own `ZDOTDIR` (zsh) or `--rcfile` (bash) that points at that tree's startup files. Measuring the live config picks up whatever the user changed since.
    12	- Run warmup rounds. The first start after a change rebuilds caches such as the completion dump, and later starts reuse them.
    13	- `-i -c exit` stops before the first prompt. Work deferred to `precmd` hooks or a deferred loader escapes it, even though the user waits for it. When deferred work matters, measure time to first prompt with a tool built for it, such as [`zsh-bench`](https://github.com/romkatv/zsh-bench), which drives a real terminal and reports first-prompt and first-command latency.
    14	- Check the project for an existing startup benchmark before building one. A harness the user already trusts sets the scenario.
    15	
    16	## Fast Signals
    17	
    18	Count processes forked during startup with the xtrace or a system tracer ([the profile skill's shell reference](../../profile/references/shell.md)). The count is deterministic, and each fork removed saves a few milliseconds.

1	---
     2	name: performance:hill-climb
     3	description: >-
     4	  Use when asked to hill-climb a program, or to make software faster or
     5	  leaner (runtime, startup, throughput, memory, bundle size) through repeated
     6	  measured changes, including resuming a climb from its notes file. For
     7	  prompts or skills scored by an eval suite, use evals:hill-climb.
     8	argument-hint: "<target> [<notes file>]"
     9	---
    10	
    11	# Hill Climb
    12	
    13	Goal: a program that is measurably better on the metric the user cares about, where every accepted change carries evidence that it beat run-to-run noise, kept behavior identical, and holds on inputs the climb never tuned against. The user stays in the loop at fixed checkpoints and can reconstruct every decision from one notes file.
    14	
    15	This skill is the workflow. Load `performance:benchmark` to build the harness and compare arms, and `performance:profile` to find where the time goes. A repo's own benchmark conventions take precedence over the defaults here.
    16	
    17	## Arguments
    18	
    19	- `<target>`: the program or command to climb. Required.
    20	- `<notes file>`: where the climb log lives. Default: `CLIMB.md` beside the benchmark harness, or `tmp/climb.md` when the repo has no harness directory. When it already exists, resume from it: skip the Frame items its Rules settle, and keep the line under its title that tells a later session to load this skill.
    21	
    22	## Frame
    23	
    24	Interview the user until each item below is settled and none rests on your assumption:
    25	
    26	- Ask in rounds with `AskUserQuestion`, one question per open decision.
    27	- Settle every item before building anything.
    28	- Write the answers into the notes file's Rules section ([references/notes.md](references/notes.md) has the template), then confirm the section with the user.
    29	- A dispatching brief settles only the items it states. Ask the rest.
    30	- When the session is unattended (a dispatched brief, or the user said they are away), settle each open item yourself. Record it in Rules as `assumed: <value>`, and name every assumed item in the first decision report.
    31	
    32	- **Metric.** The number the user cares about, on an exact scenario: the command, its input state, and the machine state. "Wall time of a sync run by hand right after one upstream commit" is a metric. "Make it faster" is not.
    33	  - Start from who waits on the result and when: a person after a change, a CI job, a scheduled run. Measure the run the user waits through, even when the code handles another run more often.
    34	  - A scheduled run nobody waits on can take on work that speeds the waited-on one.
    35	  - Ask where the real workload spends its time. A benchmark input can skip the phase users wait through.
    36	  - A memory metric is peak RSS of the scenario, compared with `compare.ts report --metric memory`. Allocation volume can be a fast signal only after the baseline shows it tracks the peak.
    37	- **Ceiling.** The value past which further gains stop mattering to the user. The climb stops there.
    38	- **Fast signal.** A cheaper or lower-noise number that moves with the metric: CPU time, instructions retired, work per tick, bytes. Accept on it only after the baseline shows it tracks the metric.
    39	- **Guard.** What must stay identical: output, final state, exit code. Name the check that proves it.
    40	  - When a candidate can change lookup order (`PATH`, module or library search paths), the guard compares what each name resolves to.
    41	  - Only the user relaxes a guard.
    42	- **Side effects.** Everything a run touches outside itself: network, remote state, installed files, caches. Decide per item whether to stub it, hold it fixed, or reset it before each run.
    43	- **Scope.** Which changes are allowed: code, config, dependencies, external tools, public API. Ask whether parallelism is in scope. When caching is in scope, ask where a cache may live and how it invalidates. Ask how much added code a gain must pay for.
    44	- **Inputs.** Which scenarios are `dev` (tuned against) and which are `holdout` (scored once at the end). Cover the workload's range of sizes and shapes. Prefer real inputs over synthetic ones for `holdout`, and look for larger real data when every `dev` input is small.
    45	- **Budget.** How long the climb may run and how the user wants progress between checkpoints.
    46	
    47	## Workspace
    48	
    49	- **herdr.** Under `HERDR_ENV=1`, run the whole climb in one herdr workspace so the user can watch every run. On a cloud VM, create it on the VM's herdr machine and add `--machine <label>` to the same commands. Load `herdr:herdr` for them.
    50	- **Runs.** Build arms per `performance:benchmark`. Launch a run longer than a few minutes detached, in the herdr pane or under `nohup`, so a session reload leaves it running. Run timed commands in the herdr pane when there is one, since the sandbox breaks ptys and skews timing.
    51	- **Progress.** `tee` every long run into a log beside the notes file. `compare.ts run` prints each round's per-arm medians. Report each decision with its numbers as it lands, and stay quiet between decisions unless an estimate slips.
    52	
    53	## Harness
    54	
    55	Build the benchmark per `performance:benchmark`, or adopt the project's own when it meets that skill's requirements. When the metric is a CI run, read [references/ci.md](references/ci.md). Then, before the baseline:
    56	
    57	- **Audit.** Check the harness against the Frame's scenario:
    58	  - It runs to the end point the user waits for. A shell benchmark that exits before the first prompt skips everything deferred to it.
    59	  - It runs the build users run, from a cache no warmer than the scenario's.
    60	- **Watchers.** When runs or resets write many files, look for processes watching the filesystem (backup, indexing, sync clients). Ask the user to exclude the harness directory.
    61	- **Isolation.** Run the program twice from a fresh reset and diff the end states. A difference is state the reset misses or a side effect leaking out.
    62	- **Tight loop.** Each run's cost repeats across every A/A, candidate, and re-baseline.
    63	  - Reset per run only the state the scenario depends on.
    64	  - Hoist work that feeds every run identically into `--setup`: fixture builds, toolchain installs, downloads and inputs the metric does not cover.
    65	  - Repeat the end-state diff after each hoist. Return a step to the reset when the diff or the A/A shifts.
    66	- **Cost.** Time one run with its reset and multiply by the A/A's run count. When that takes a large share of the budget, tighten the reset or cut runs first.
    67	- **Baseline.** Record the unchanged program twice (an A/A comparison). Its spread is the noise floor and sets the run count a candidate needs.
    68	- **Profile.** Profile the baseline per `performance:profile` and rank where the time goes.
    69	  - Size runner and config options (parallelism, caching flags) too, so the candidate list ranks them beside code changes.
    70	  - Confirm the program reads a config option before measuring it. Some tools ignore an unknown key without a warning.
    71	
    72	#### Checkpoint
    73	
    74	Show the user the baseline table, the noise floor, the profile's top entries, a candidate list ranked by the share of the metric each one targets, and the Set Aside leads. When the user is present, wait for the review before the first candidate. When the session is unattended, write the checkpoint into the notes file and continue.
    75	
    76	## Loop
    77	
    78	#### Candidate
    79	
    80	Make one change per candidate. Before measuring it, append to the notes file, so the decision cannot be fitted to whichever number happened to move:
    81	
    82	- The hypothesis, citing the profile entry it targets.
    83	- The target: which metric moves, and in which direction.
    84	- The guards a side effect would hit.
    85	
    86	Write the change for the workload, never for a `dev` input's specifics (its sizes, paths, or contents). A fast path keyed on the fixture passes `dev` and loses on `holdout`.
    87	
    88	A candidate without a profile entry behind it ranks last, unless a measurement sizes the time it targets: the gap between wall and CPU time, or a cold run against the warm one profiled. Rank that candidate at its measured size.
    89	
    90	Record every lead you do not climb in the notes file's Set Aside table with its reason. Drop a lead the user put in scope only after asking.
    91	
    92	#### Measure
    93	
    94	Run the guard check first. A candidate that changes behavior is rejected without timing.
    95	
    96	Screen with the fast signal or a microbenchmark of the changed path. Confirm a candidate that passes the screen with the full metric, interleaved against the current accepted arm at the baseline's run count. Confirm on every `dev` scenario, including ones the change cannot reach on paper, since a shared lock, allocator, or cache carries a change into code it never touches.
    97	
    98	#### Decide
    99	
   100	- **Accept** when the target moves in the predicted direction past the acceptance rule in the notes file (default: permutation p < 0.1 and a median gain of at least 3%) and no guard regresses, and the gain pays for the code the change adds at the Scope's bar. Commit the change alone, with the evidence in the commit body.
   101	- **Keep unconfirmed** when the target did not move but the user agrees to keep the change for a reason outside the metric. Label it "kept, unconfirmed" in the notes, commit body, and PR, and leave it out of the reported gain.
   102	- **Keep as a trade** when the target improves, another metric regresses, and the user approves the trade. Label it "kept, trade" and report both numbers wherever the gain appears.
   103	- **Reject** otherwise. Record the hypothesis, pseudocode of the change, and the numbers in the notes file, and save the diff as a patch beside it, so the null result stays findable. A rejected hypothesis stays rejected until a new profile argues for it.
   104	- **Re-run** an accept that rests on rounds `compare.ts report` flags for load, and decide on the re-run. An accept rests on them when the gain or its significance fails without those rounds.
   105	- **Bound** an accepted gain by its target's time in the profile. Re-measure a gain past that bound before committing, or report the excess as unexplained.
   106	
   107	After each decision:
   108	
   109	- Re-profile after an accept, since the ranking shifts.
   110	- Report the first decision to the user in one line, and continue unless the user redirects.
   111	- Past the Checkpoint, ask with `AskUserQuestion` only to change the Scope, a Guard, or the Ceiling. Decide anything else, record it in the notes as `assumed: <value>`, and name it in the next report.
   112	- Commit a mid-climb harness change separately, re-run the baseline and the A/A, and note it in the notes file. A new input family, inputs at a new scale, and a new runtime or dependency version are harness changes.
   113	- After two rejections in a row, re-run the A/A and re-profile before the next candidate. A stall often means the noise floor rose or the profile ranks work the scenario does not wait on.
   114	
   115	## Stopping
   116	
   117	Before stopping on anything but the ceiling or the budget, profile every Frame metric at head on the largest inputs, and rank what that profile shows. A climb that has accepted most of its candidates still has headroom.
   118	
   119	Stop when any of these holds, and say which:
   120	
   121	- The metric reached the ceiling.
   122	- A third candidate in a row was rejected after that A/A and re-profile.
   123	- The profile's remaining entries are outside the Frame's scope.
   124	- The budget cannot cover another candidate at the baseline's run count while leaving time for the holdout and the report.
   125	
   126	When an ETA was given, re-estimate it after each decision, counting the validation runs still ahead. Tell the user as soon as the estimate slips.
   127	
   128	Then run `holdout` once on the original base and the final commit. The climb holds when no holdout case is significantly worse. Report every holdout case whose median rose, with its p, as a slip. A `dev` gain with a flat or falling `holdout` overfit the `dev` inputs.
   129	
   130	## Report
   131	
   132	- **Notes.** Finish the Where It Stands section: base against final on every scenario, starred where significant, and the stop reason.
   133	- **PR or maintainer comment.** Lead with the metric's before and after in plain words, naming the base commit measured against. Round the numbers in prose, and give exact figures in the tables. Then list the accepted changes with each one's gain. Put one metric per table column.
   134	- **Artifacts.** Ship the code changes alone. Add the harness, notes, or generated data (timings, caches) only when the user asks. On a repo the user does not own, summarize each rejected candidate in a few lines, without links to files that do not ship.
   135	- **Artifact.** Offer to publish the notes when others will read them.

1	# CI Climbs
     2	
     3	Read this when the metric is a CI run: a job's or workflow's wall time, a critical path, a cache restore. The harness is a dispatched workflow. Each run costs minutes of runner time and writes to state other branches share.
     4	
     5	## Harness
     6	
     7	- Dispatch each arm as its own workflow run on a measurement branch, from the same base commit. Record each run's ID and the base commit in the notes file.
     8	- Profile from step timings, job logs, and trace artifacts. Count runner queue wait separately from job time, since it is noise the change cannot touch.
     9	- Run the A/A on the same branch setup and runner pool as the candidates.
    10	- Re-baseline whenever the base branch moves or its caches are re-saved. A candidate measured against a days-old base cache and one measured after a re-save are different scenarios, and chaining their numbers into one headline overstates the gain.
    11	- A round takes 20 to 40 minutes. Set the run count from the A/A and size the Budget in runner time before the first candidate.
    12	
    13	## Shared Quotas
    14	
    15	Caches, artifact storage, and API rate limits are shared with every other branch. A measurement that pushes one past its cap evicts or throttles the default branch, and every PR runs slower until the default branch saves again.
    16	
    17	- Before the first run, read the repo's current cache and artifact usage against the cap.
    18	- Size the measurement against runs × artifact size, and keep the total under the remaining headroom.
    19	- Delete each arm's caches and artifacts once its results are recorded.
    20	- Ask the user before any run that would cross the cap.
    21	
    22	## Cold Branches
    23	
    24	Caches are usually scoped per branch, so a new candidate branch starts cold while the base branch restores warm. Match cache state across arms: seed each measurement branch from the base branch's cache, or measure every arm cold. Name which in Rules.
    25	
    26	## Holdout
    27	
    28	Real PR runs on the default branch after the merge are the holdout. List the post-merge run IDs and compare their critical path with the final measurement, excluding PRs that change the cached inputs themselves.

1 # Climb Notes 2 3 The notes file is the climb's single record. A reader who was not in the session reconstructs every decision from it: what was measured, how, what was tried, and why each change was kept or dropped. Write it as the climb runs, never from memory at the end. 4 5 ## Template 6 7 ````markdown 8 # Performance Climb 9 10 Climbed with `/performance:hill-climb`. A session resuming this climb invokes that skill before its next candidate. 11 12 13 14 ## Rules 15 16 - Metric: . 17 - Ceiling: . 18 - Fast signal: . 19 - Guard: . 20 - Side effects: . 21 - Scope: . 22 - Inputs: `dev` , every one run to confirm an accept. `holdout` , scored once at the end. 23 - Acceptance: . 24 - Stop: . 25 26 Mark an item the user never answered as `assumed: `. 27 28 ## Harness 29 30 31 32 ## Baseline 33 34 35 36 ## Profile 37 38 39 40 ## Set Aside 41 42 | Lead | Profile entry | Reason | 43 | --- | --- | --- | 44 | | | | 45 46 ## Candidates 47 48 ### : (``) 49 50 Hypothesis: . 51 52 ``` 53 before: 54 after: 55 ``` 56 57 Target: . Guards: . Guard check: . 58 59 | Scenario | base | candidate | change | 60 | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | 61 | | | | <±%> (p=

)* | 62 63 64 65 ## Where It Stands 66 67 68 ```` 69 70 ## Conventions 71 72 - Star a cell whose difference clears the acceptance test. An unstarred difference is a tie, however large it looks. 73 - Keep pseudocode to the lines that changed. A reader should see the idea without opening the diff. 74 - Link each comparison's raw results (for example `hyperfine --export-json` files) beside the table that summarizes them. 75 - Record a harness change as its own entry under Harness with the re-run baseline, since every later number rests on it.

1	---
     2	name: performance:profile
     3	description: >-
     4	  Use when asked why a program, script, or web page is slow or memory-heavy,
     5	  or what dominates its runtime, before deciding what to change.
     6	argument-hint: "<command | url>"
     7	---
     8	
     9	# Profile
    10	
    11	Goal: a ranked, readable list of where the program's time or peak memory goes on the scenario the user cares about, with each entry's share of the total. Every optimization decision rests on that list, so it must come from a measurement of the real scenario.
    12	
    13	## Tools
    14	
    15	- `samply`: !`samply --version 2>/dev/null || echo "not found. Required for native and whole-process profiles."`
    16	- `hyperfine`: !`hyperfine --version 2>/dev/null || echo "not found. Needed for the wall/CPU split."`
    17	- `bun`: !`bun --version 2>/dev/null || echo "not found."`
    18	- `node`: !`node --version 2>/dev/null || echo "not found."`
    19	- `agent-browser`: !`agent-browser --version 2>/dev/null || echo "not found. Required for web apps."`
    20	- `py-spy`: !`py-spy --version 2>/dev/null || echo "not found. Needed only for Python."`
    21	- `malloc_history`: !`command -v malloc_history >/dev/null && echo found || echo "not found. Needed for native memory on macOS."`
    22	- `heaptrack`: !`heaptrack --version 2>/dev/null || echo "not found. Needed for native memory on Linux."`
    23	
    24	When a required tool is missing and the project's own tooling does not cover its job, tell the user which one, then stop.
    25	
    26	## Existing Tooling
    27	
    28	Look for the project's own profiling setup before recording one: profiling scripts, an environment variable that turns on a profiler, a formatter for profiler output. Use it when it meets the requirements the references below are built to meet:
    29	
    30	- **Scenario.** It profiles the scenario and build the user runs.
    31	- **Ranking.** It ranks entries by self and inclusive time with each one's share, or writes a file that a summarizer or viewer ranks.
    32	- **Coverage.** It covers every process the scenario spawns, and time spent waiting when wall time exceeds CPU.
    33	
    34	When it misses some, use it for what it covers and add a profiler from the references for the rest.
    35	
    36	## Split Wall From CPU
    37	
    38	Run the scenario once under `hyperfine --runs 3` and compare wall time with user plus system CPU.
    39	
    40	- **CPU-bound** (CPU near wall): a sampling profiler finds the hot functions.
    41	- **Waiting** (wall well above CPU): the time goes to network, disk, child processes, locks, or sleeps. Find what it waits on: which child process runs longest, which request is slow. A CPU profile of a waiting program ranks the wrong things.
    42	
    43	## Pick the Profiler
    44	
    45	Profile the same scenario the benchmark measures, from the same starting state. The references call bundled scripts under `<skill-dir>`, which is `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}`. Read the reference for the program's platform:
    46	
    47	- Any native executable, or a whole process tree: [references/samply.md](references/samply.md). It follows child processes, so it also answers which child a waiting program waits on.
    48	- TypeScript or JavaScript on Bun or Node: [references/javascript.md](references/javascript.md).
    49	- Go: [references/go.md](references/go.md).
    50	- Rust: [references/rust.md](references/rust.md).
    51	- A web app in a browser: [references/browser.md](references/browser.md).
    52	- A shell script: [references/shell.md](references/shell.md).
    53	- Python: [references/python.md](references/python.md).
    54	
    55	When the question is memory, read [references/memory.md](references/memory.md) for native code. Runtimes with a garbage collector have their own heap profilers in the language references.
    56	
    57	When macOS blocks the profiler or the metric needs hardware counters, read [references/linux-vm.md](references/linux-vm.md).
    58	
    59	## Report
    60	
    61	Write the ranking as a table: entry (function, process, or phase), its time or bytes at peak, and its share of the scenario's total. Name the tool and the scenario that produced it. Keep the raw profile file beside the table so the user can open it in its viewer.
    62	
    63	A profile finds candidates. It does not show that fixing one moves the metric. Hand the list to `performance:benchmark` or `performance:hill-climb` to measure a change.
    64	
    65	## Gotchas
    66	
    67	- A profiler's overhead falls unevenly: a per-command trace inflates many cheap commands far more than a few expensive ones. Time each suspect alone without the profiler to rank and bound it.
    68	- Sampling profilers record no allocations. A memory question needs an allocation profiler ranked at the peak, not a CPU profile or total allocation volume.
    69	- Compare the profile's total span with the metric. A span well short of the metric means the profile missed part of the scenario, such as a config file that never loaded.
    70	- A profile of a debug build, a warm cache the real scenario lacks, or a tiny input ranks the wrong hot spots. Match the scenario.
    71	- On macOS, profilers cannot attach to SIP-protected system binaries (`/bin/sh`, `/usr/bin/*`). Run the program through an interpreter or binary outside those directories, or move the run into a Linux VM ([references/linux-vm.md](references/linux-vm.md)).

1	# Browser
     2	
     3	Profile a web app with the `agent-browser` CLI, which drives a real Chrome and records Chrome DevTools traces. Load an `agent-browser` skill for session and command details when one is installed, or read `agent-browser --help`.
     4	
     5	## Record
     6	
     7	```bash
     8	agent-browser profiler start
     9	# drive the scenario: navigate, click, type, scroll
    10	agent-browser profiler stop tmp/profile/<name>.json
    11	```
    12	
    13	The file is a Chrome trace. The user opens it in the DevTools Performance panel or [Perfetto](https://ui.perfetto.dev). Pass `--categories` to narrow what the trace records when the file gets large.
    14	
    15	For React apps, `agent-browser react renders` counts component renders, and `--json` gives a machine-readable count per component.
    16	
    17	## Reading It
    18	
    19	- Rank main-thread time by task type: scripting, style and layout, paint, idle. A main thread that stays busy longer than about 50 ms at a stretch blocks input.
    20	- For animation or streaming UI, count frames over the budget (16.7 ms at 60 Hz) and report the worst ones.
    21	- Network waterfalls answer load-time questions. The CPU profile answers interaction questions. Pick the one matching the scenario.
    22	
    23	## Deterministic Signals
    24	
    25	Browser wall time is noisy. Deterministic counts make better fast signals: renders per component, layout count, long tasks, DOM nodes, bytes transferred. Check each against wall time on the baseline before trusting it.
    26	
    27	## Gotchas
    28	
    29	- A development build (React dev mode, unminified bundles, profiling builds) inflates and reshapes the profile. Profile a production build, or say which build it was.
    30	- Throttle the CPU through CDP (`Emulation.setCPUThrottlingRate`) to mimic slower user hardware. A fast laptop hides work that users feel.
    31	- Extensions, an open DevTools panel, and a warm HTTP cache all change the result. Record in a clean profile with the cache state the scenario calls for.

1	# Go
     2	
     3	Go ships its profiler in the toolchain. `pprof` names Go functions with source lines and prints text rankings directly.
     4	
     5	## CPU and Memory
     6	
     7	Profile a benchmark or test with flags:
     8	
     9	```bash
    10	go test -run '^$' -bench <Name> -cpuprofile tmp/profile/cpu.prof -memprofile tmp/profile/mem.prof ./<pkg>
    11	```
    12	
    13	Profile a whole program by starting `runtime/pprof` in `main` (`pprof.StartCPUProfile` / `StopCPUProfile`), or by importing `net/http/pprof` in a long-running server and fetching `/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30`.
    14	
    15	Read the ranking as text:
    16	
    17	```bash
    18	go tool pprof -top -nodecount=25 tmp/profile/cpu.prof
    19	go tool pprof -top -cum -nodecount=25 tmp/profile/cpu.prof
    20	go tool pprof -list '<func regex>' tmp/profile/cpu.prof
    21	```
    22	
    23	`-top` sorts by self time, `-cum` by inclusive time, and `-list` annotates a function's source line by line. For memory, add `-sample_index=alloc_space` to rank allocation volume, which drives GC time, or `inuse_space` for what stays live. Point the user at `go tool pprof -http=:0 <file>` for the flame graph.
    24	
    25	## Waiting
    26	
    27	A CPU profile misses time a goroutine spends blocked.
    28	
    29	- `-blockprofile` and `-mutexprofile` on `go test` rank where goroutines wait on channels, locks, and `select`.
    30	- `go test -trace tmp/profile/trace.out` (or `runtime/trace` in `main`) records scheduling, syscalls, and GC per goroutine. `go tool trace` opens it in a browser for the user.
    31	
    32	## Startup
    33	
    34	`GODEBUG=inittrace=1 <binary>` prints the time and allocations of each package's `init`. Run the built binary, since `go run` adds a compile to every start.
    35	
    36	## Gotchas
    37	
    38	- `samply` also profiles Go binaries and follows child processes. Use it when the program shells out.
    39	- A profile of a benchmark with a tiny input ranks setup and loop overhead. Match the scenario.

1	# JavaScript and TypeScript
     2	
     3	The runtime's own profiler names JavaScript functions with source locations. `samply` shows the same code as JIT addresses, so use it only for native time and child processes.
     4	
     5	## Bun
     6	
     7	```bash
     8	bun --cpu-prof-md --cpu-prof-dir tmp/profile <script.ts> [args]
     9	```
    10	
    11	`--cpu-prof-md` writes the profile as markdown built for reading in a model's context: hot functions with self and total time and their source locations. Read that file directly.
    12	
    13	- `--cpu-prof` writes a `.cpuprofile` for Chrome DevTools or `speedscope`. Keep one beside the markdown for the user.
    14	- `--cpu-prof-interval <µs>` samples more often for a short script.
    15	- `--heap-prof` records allocations when the question is memory.
    16	- The profile covers one Bun process. A script that spawns Bun children needs the flag passed to each, or `samply` over the whole tree.
    17	
    18	## Node
    19	
    20	```bash
